name: What Is Geology?
teaser: Geology is the science of the solid Earth: its rocks, minerals, processes, and 4.6-billion-year history. Geologists read the planet's story in layers of stone, from the shifting of continents to clues of ancient climates. The field spans volcanoes, earthquakes, groundwater, and resources. Every rock outcrop is a page of Earth's autobiography, and geology is the discipline that learns to read it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what geologists study and why rocks tell stories, then explain how geology connects to everyday life.

name: What Geologists Do
teaser: Geologists study the Earth's materials and history: they map rocks, hunt for resources, monitor hazards, and read the deep past from layers of stone. Some work in oil and mining, others in environmental protection or academia. Fieldwork means hammering outcrops and recording layers; lab work means analyzing minerals and fossils. The job is part scientist, part detective, and always grounded.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the daily work of geologists from field to lab, then explain why they care about deep time.

name: The Rock Cycle
teaser: The rock cycle is Earth's great recycling system: igneous rocks form from cooling magma, weathering and erosion break them into sediment, compaction turns sediment into sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure transform either into metamorphic rock — which can melt and begin again. The cycle never stops; it just runs on geological time. Any rock can become any other, given the right conditions.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks turn into each other, then explain what drives the cycle.

name: Deep Time
teaser: Deep time is the dizzying scale of Earth's 4.6-billion-year history: human history is a blink on this timeline. Geologists learn to think in millions and billions of years, where continents drift, mountains rise and erode, and species come and go. The concept, established in the 1800s, freed geology from the limits of written history. Deep time is geology's gift — a humbling sense of scale.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how geologists think in millions of years, then explain why the human lifespan is a blink on that scale.

name: Uniformitarianism
teaser: Uniformitarianism is geology's founding principle: the same natural processes operating today — erosion, deposition, volcanism — operated in the past at similar rates. Coined as 'the present is the key to the past' by James Hutton and popularized by Charles Lyell, it lets geologists interpret ancient rocks by studying modern processes. It replaced catastrophism and made Earth history scientifically readable.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Hutton's idea that slow processes built today's landscapes, then explain how it differs from catastrophism.

name: Catastrophism
teaser: Catastrophism held that Earth's features were shaped by sudden, violent events — floods, upheavals, divine acts — rather than slow processes. It dominated early geology and was later refined, not abandoned: modern science recognizes both gradual change and rare catastrophes, from asteroid impacts to massive volcanic eruptions. The debate taught geologists to weigh the evidence. Today, catastrophism survives as a complement to uniformitarianism.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how floods and impacts reshape landscapes fast, then explain how modern geology blends both views.

name: Strata
teaser: Strata are the layers of sedimentary rock that record Earth's history: each layer was deposited as sediment, then hardened, and later layers stacked on top. Strata preserve fossils, ripple marks, and chemical clues of their time. The law of superposition — oldest at the bottom — makes strata a timeline. Reading strata is how geologists reconstruct ancient landscapes and life.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how sediment layers stack like pages of history, then explain what a stratum is.

name: The Geologic Time Scale
teaser: The geologic time scale divides Earth's 4.6-billion-year history into eons, eras, periods, and epochs, each marked by major changes in rocks and life: the Precambrian's long microbial age, the Paleozoic's early life and mass extinctions, the Mesozoic's dinosaurs, and the Cenozoic's mammals. The boundaries are set by real events in the rock record. It's the calendar of deep time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how geologists divide Earth history into eons and eras, then explain which era we live in.

name: Geologic Eras
teaser: Geologic eras are the big chapters of Earth history: the Paleozoic — 'ancient life' — saw marine life explode and the first land plants and animals; the Mesozoic — 'middle life' — was the age of dinosaurs; and the Cenozoic — 'recent life' — brought mammals and eventually humans. Each era spans hundreds of millions of years and ends with major change. Eras help geologists think about deep time at a human scale.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the Phanerozoic eras and their life, then explain why the Paleozoic is named for ancient life.

name: Fossils
teaser: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient life: shells, bones, teeth, imprints, and footprints. Most form when organisms are buried quickly in sediment, and minerals slowly replace or fill their remains. Fossils document evolution, date rock layers, and reveal ancient environments. They're the only direct record of life's history, and geologists treat them as the clockwork of the rock record.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fossils form and what they reveal, then explain why most organisms never fossilize.

name: Radiometric Dating
teaser: Radiometric dating measures the age of rocks using radioactive decay: elements like uranium and potassium decay into daughter isotopes at known, constant rates — half-lives. By measuring the ratio of parent to daughter atoms, geologists calculate when the rock formed. It works for anything from volcanic ash to the oldest minerals on Earth. Radiometric dating gave geology its absolute clock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how radioactive decay reveals rock ages, then explain what a half-life is.

name: Half-Lives
teaser: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive isotope to decay: it's constant for each isotope — carbon-14 takes 5,730 years, potassium-40 about 1.25 billion, uranium-238 about 4.5 billion. After one half-life half remains, after two a quarter, and so on. Geologists measure this ratio to date rocks and fossils. Half-lives are the built-in clocks of the natural world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why half-lives are constant, then explain how they allow dating across deep time.

name: Relative Dating
teaser: Relative dating orders events without giving exact ages: the law of superposition says lower layers are older, cross-cutting relationships say a fault or intrusion is younger than the rock it cuts, and inclusions are older than the rock containing them. Fossils add order through succession. Relative dating was geology's original timeline, still essential alongside radiometric methods.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how superposition and cross-cutting order events, then explain what the law of superposition says.

name: Index Fossils
teaser: Index fossils are species that lived briefly but spread widely, making them perfect time markers: trilobites, ammonites, and certain graptolites each define a slice of geologic time. Find the same index fossil in rocks on different continents and the layers are the same age. Index fossils were how geologists correlated strata before radiometric dating. They're nature's own geological clocks.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why some fossils date layers precisely, then explain what makes a good index fossil.

name: Unconformities
teaser: An unconformity is a gap in the rock record — a buried surface of erosion or nondeposition: it marks missing time where layers were removed or never formed, often because sea level fell or land rose. Siccar Point, where James Hutton recognized one, is famous. Unconformities remind geologists that the record is incomplete: Earth's history has many erased chapters.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how gaps in the rock record form, then explain what an angular unconformity is.

name: Geology Tools
teaser: Geologists' tools are simple and durable: a rock hammer for splitting stone, a hand lens for examining crystals, a compass and map for orientation, and acid for testing carbonates. Modern gear adds GPS, drones, and geophysical instruments. The classic kit has barely changed in a century because the core skill is observation. Tools help, but the geologist's eye is the real instrument.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the tools geologists use from hammers to drones, then explain what a hand lens is for.

name: Geological Fieldwork
teaser: Geological fieldwork is where the science is born: geologists walk outcrops, hammer samples, measure layers, and map structures, recording everything in field notebooks. They trace formations across hills, log drill cores, and collect fossils and minerals. Fieldwork is physical and weather-dependent, but it's irreplaceable — rocks reveal their secrets best in place. The map and notebook are the geologist's canvas.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why geologists spend so much time outdoors, then explain what mapping outcrops reveals.

name: Geologic Maps
teaser: Geologic maps show what's beneath the surface: colors mark rock units, symbols show faults and folds, and patterns record age and structure. Reading one reveals the area's history — layers tilted by mountain-building, intrusions cutting old rock, river deposits on top. Geologic maps guide everything from mineral exploration to earthquake risk. They compress millions of years into a single sheet.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how maps show rock types and ages, then explain what a strike and dip is.

name: Earth's Systems
teaser: Earth is a set of interacting systems: the geosphere of rock and interior, the hydrosphere of water, the atmosphere, the biosphere of life, and the cryosphere of ice. Geology studies how these systems exchange energy and matter — volcanoes feeding the atmosphere, rivers moving sediment, life reshaping rock. The systems connect across time scales. Understanding Earth means following the connections.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere interact, then explain why geology touches them all.

name: Why Geology Matters
teaser: Geology matters because civilization runs on it: every metal, mineral, and fuel comes from the ground, and every city sits on geologic foundations. Geology protects lives through hazard warnings, finds water, and guides energy and climate decisions. It also answers the big questions — where we came from and how the planet works. Geology is the science under everything else.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how geology provides resources and safety, then explain how it helps plan cities.

name: Minerals
teaser: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure: quartz is silica, salt is sodium chloride, diamond is pure carbon. They form through cooling magma, precipitation from water, or changes under heat and pressure. Minerals are the building blocks of rocks and the raw materials of civilization. About 5,000 are known, each with its own recipe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what makes something a mineral, then explain the difference between a mineral and a rock.

name: Mineral Properties
teaser: Minerals are identified by their properties: hardness, color, streak, luster, cleavage, and crystal form. Streak — the color of the powdered mineral — often reveals identity better than color itself. Hardness is tested by what scratches what, and cleavage shows how crystals break along planes. Together the properties fingerprint a mineral. A hand lens and a few simple tests identify most specimens.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the properties geologists test, then explain why streak beats color for identification.

name: Mohs Hardness Scale
teaser: The Mohs hardness scale ranks minerals from 1 to 10 by what scratches what: talc is 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, feldspar 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, and diamond 10. Each mineral scratches everything below it. A fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin 3.5, and a knife blade 5.5. The scale turns a simple test into identification.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how minerals are ranked 1 to 10 by hardness, then explain why diamond tops the scale.

name: Cleavage and Fracture
teaser: Cleavage is a mineral's tendency to break along flat planes where its atomic bonds are weak: mica cleaves into thin sheets, halite into cubes, calcite into rhombs. Fracture, by contrast, is irregular breaking — quartz and glass fracture like broken pottery. Cleavage reflects internal crystal structure, so it's a powerful identification tool. A mineral's breaking habit reveals its atomic architecture.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why some minerals split along flat planes, then explain the difference from fracture.

name: Crystal Systems
teaser: Crystal systems classify minerals by their symmetry: cubic crystals like salt and pyrite grow as cubes, hexagonal like quartz and beryl as six-sided prisms, and triclinic crystals with no symmetry at all. The system is set by the arrangement of atoms and the angles between crystal faces. Each mineral grows in its own system. Crystal shape is geometry written in atoms.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how minerals grow in seven crystal systems, then explain what a crystal habit is.

name: How Crystals Grow
teaser: Crystals grow when atoms or molecules lock into an orderly repeating pattern: from cooling magma, evaporating brine, or mineral-rich water. Growth needs space and time — crowded conditions produce masses of small crystals, open cavities allow large, perfect ones. Each mineral has a characteristic shape set by its atomic structure. A crystal is nature's most precise construction project.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how cooling and space shape crystals, then explain why crystals have flat faces.

name: Quartz
teaser: Quartz is the most common mineral in Earth's crust: pure silicon dioxide, it's the main ingredient of sand and sandstone, and it crystallizes into hexagonal prisms. It comes in many varieties — clear rock crystal, purple amethyst, smoky quartz, and pink rose quartz. Quartz is hard, stable, and chemically simple, and it powers clocks and electronics through its piezoelectric effect.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why quartz is everywhere, then explain its many colors and varieties.

name: Feldspar
teaser: Feldspar is the most abundant mineral group in the crust, making up about 60% of Earth's rocks: it's a family of aluminosilicates with potassium, sodium, or calcium — orthoclase is pink, plagioclase is white or gray. Feldspar is a key ingredient of granite and basalt, and it weathers into clay, feeding soils. When rock breaks down, feldspar becomes the fine material that holds water and nutrients.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why feldspar is so abundant, then explain its role in granite.

name: Mica
teaser: Mica is a sheet silicate that splits into paper-thin, flexible layers: its atomic structure has planes of weakly bonded sheets, so it cleaves perfectly into transparent flakes. Biotite is black, muscovite is silvery and nearly clear. Mica resists heat and electricity, so it's used in electronics and insulation. Its perfect cleavage makes it one of the most recognizable minerals in any rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why mica peels into thin sheets, then explain its uses in electronics.

name: Calcite
teaser: Calcite is calcium carbonate, the mineral of limestone and marble: it fizzes in acid — a quick field test — and cleaves into rhombohedrons. Calcite is everywhere: it forms the shells of sea creatures, builds cave stalactites, and makes the white cliffs of Dover. It's used in cement, glass, and antacids. Its double refraction means images seen through a clear crystal appear doubled.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how calcite forms and fizzes, then explain why it matters for building.

name: Gold
teaser: Gold is the metal that launched civilizations: it's dense, soft, and chemically inert, so it doesn't tarnish or corrode — which is why it's been jewelry and currency for thousands of years. Gold forms in veins from hot fluids and in placer deposits where streams concentrate the heavy grains. Most gold mined today comes from microscopic particles in hard rock. Its chemistry makes it both beautiful and practical.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why gold forms in veins and placer deposits, then explain why it does not tarnish.

name: Diamond
teaser: Diamond is carbon in its hardest natural form: under enormous heat and pressure deep in Earth, carbon atoms bond into a rigid three-dimensional lattice, making diamond the hardest known natural material. It's formed about 150 kilometers down and carried up by volcanic pipes. Most diamonds are industrial — used for cutting and drilling — while rare flawless ones become gems. Its toughness is pure atomic structure.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how diamonds form deep in the mantle, then explain the difference from graphite.

name: Graphite
teaser: Graphite is carbon's soft cousin: its atoms bond in flat sheets that slide past each other, which is why pencil lead writes and graphite lubricates. The sheets conduct electricity, making graphite essential in batteries and electronics. It forms under moderate heat and pressure in metamorphic rock. The same element as diamond, arranged differently — graphite's chemistry is all about structure.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why graphite is soft while diamond is hard, then explain its use in batteries.

name: Halite
teaser: Halite — rock salt — is sodium chloride, one of the most common minerals on Earth: it forms cubic crystals when salty water evaporates, creating thick deposits where ancient seas dried up. Salt has been prized for seasoning and preserving food for millennia, and the word 'salary' comes from it. Modern uses range from road deicing to chemical production. It's the mineral civilization couldn't live without.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how salt deposits form, then explain why salt was once worth its weight in gold.

name: Gypsum
teaser: Gypsum is a soft sulfate mineral — hydrated calcium sulfate — that forms when salty water evaporates: it's the mineral behind drywall, plaster, and plaster of Paris. Its softness (2 on Mohs scale) makes it easy to carve and shape. Gypsum also forms desert roses and the giant crystals of Mexico's Cave of Crystals. When heated, it loses water and can be reshaped — the chemistry of wallboard.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how gypsum forms and dries, then explain what drywall is made of.

name: Gemstones
teaser: Gemstones are minerals prized for beauty and rarity: ruby, sapphire, emerald, diamond, opal, and hundreds more. Most gem colors come from trace impurities — chromium makes ruby red, iron makes sapphire blue. Cut and polished, they're jewelry; uncut, they're mineral specimens. Gemstones form in very specific geologic settings, from volcanic pipes to metamorphic veins. Rarity, hardness, and color set their value.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what turns a mineral into a gem, then explain the difference between precious and semi-precious.

name: Ruby and Sapphire
teaser: Ruby and sapphire are both corundum — aluminum oxide — the second-hardest natural mineral after diamond: chromium impurities turn it red and make it ruby, while iron and titanium make sapphire blue. Both form in metamorphic and igneous rocks under high heat. Burma's rubies and Kashmir's sapphires are legendary. One mineral, two gems, colored entirely by trace chemistry.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how corundum becomes ruby and sapphire, then explain what chromium adds.

name: Emerald
teaser: Emerald is the green member of the beryl family, colored by chromium and vanadium: it forms in hydrothermal veins and metamorphic rocks, often with cracks and inclusions that make it brittle. Most emeralds are oiled or resin-filled to hide flaws. Colombia's Muzo and Chivor mines have produced the finest for centuries. Its deep green makes it one of the four classic precious gems.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how emeralds form in unusual rocks, then explain why they often have inclusions.

name: Opal
teaser: Opal is hydrated silica, not a crystal: it's made of microscopic silica spheres packed in a regular array, and the gaps between spheres diffract light into shifting colors — the play of color that makes it prized. Opal forms when silica-rich water seeps into rock and dries, filling cracks and cavities. Australia produces most of the world's opal. Its colors come from structure, not pigment.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how opal traps water to make color, then explain why it is not a crystal.

name: Mineral Resources
teaser: Mineral resources are the Earth's economic storehouses: metals like copper, iron, and lithium, plus sand, gravel, salt, and phosphate. They're concentrated by geologic processes — volcanic activity, hydrothermal fluids, weathering, and evaporation. Modern civilization consumes billions of tons a year. Resource geology locates the deposits, estimates their size, and plans extraction. The periodic table is literally mined from the ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn which minerals power modern life, then explain what conflict minerals are.

name: Igneous Rocks
teaser: Igneous rocks form from cooling magma or lava: intrusive rocks like granite cool slowly underground, growing large crystals, while extrusive rocks like basalt cool quickly at the surface, with small or invisible crystals. The composition varies from silica-rich light rocks to iron-rich dark ones. Igneous rocks make up the bulk of the crust and are the starting material of the rock cycle. All rocks begin as igneous.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how magma and lava become rock, then explain the name's fiery meaning.

name: Magma
teaser: Magma is molten rock beneath the surface: a mixture of melted minerals, dissolved gases, and crystals, typically 700-1,300°C. It forms where heat and pressure allow mantle or crustal rock to melt, and it rises because it's less dense than surrounding rock. As magma cools, minerals crystallize out in order, building igneous rocks. Magma is the raw material of all new crust.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what magma is made of and why it rises, then explain the difference from lava.

name: Lava
teaser: Lava is magma that reaches the surface: it erupts from volcanoes, fissures, and vents, losing its dissolved gases as it flows and cools. Basaltic lava flows fast and thin, while silica-rich lava is thick and explosive. The temperature of lava ranges from about 700-1,200°C. As it cools, it freezes into volcanic rock. Lava is geology at its most visible — the Earth's interior, made liquid.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how magma becomes lava, then explain why lava flows at different speeds.

name: Intrusive Igneous Rocks
teaser: Intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly beneath the surface, giving minerals time to grow: granite's visible crystals and gabbro's coarse grains are the signature. They form in magma chambers, sills, and dikes, and are exposed only after erosion removes the overlying rock. Slow cooling means large crystals — the size of the crystals reveals the cooling history. Intrusive rocks are the underground architecture of volcanoes.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why slow cooling underground makes large crystals, then explain what plutonic rocks are.

name: Extrusive Igneous Rocks
teaser: Extrusive igneous rocks cool quickly at the surface, freezing small crystals: basalt's fine grains and obsidian's glassy texture form when lava chills fast. Sometimes cooling is so rapid that no crystals grow at all, producing volcanic glass. Extrusive rocks cover the ocean floor and build volcanic islands. Their fine texture records the speed of their cooling.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why quick cooling makes fine grains, then explain what volcanic rocks are.

name: Granite
teaser: Granite is the classic intrusive rock: coarse-grained, light-colored, and rich in quartz, feldspar, and mica, it cooled slowly deep underground. Its speckled look comes from the mix of minerals — pink or white feldspar, glassy quartz, dark mica. Granite is strong and attractive, making it a favorite building and countertop stone. Continental crust is largely granite.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how granite forms and why it is so common, then explain what its speckles are.

name: Basalt
teaser: Basalt is the most common volcanic rock on Earth: dark, fine-grained, and rich in iron and magnesium, it forms from fast-cooling lava. It builds the ocean floor, volcanic islands like Hawaii and Iceland, and vast flood basalt plains. Basalt's columnar joints — the Giant's Causeway's hexagonal pillars — form as it cools and contracts. Most of the planet's crust is basalt.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why basalt covers so much of the Earth, then explain its link to mid-ocean ridges.

name: Obsidian
teaser: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava that cooled so fast that no crystals formed, freezing into a black, glassy solid. It's typically rhyolitic — silica-rich — and it fractures conchoidally into razor-sharp edges, which ancient people shaped into knives and arrowheads. Obsidian reveals eruption speed: instant chilling. Because it's glass, it weathers and hydrates slowly, and old edges can even be dated by that hydration.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how lava cools into glass without crystals, then explain why ancient people prized it.

name: Pumice
teaser: Pumice is volcanic rock full of trapped gas bubbles: when gas-rich lava erupts and cools instantly, the bubbles freeze into a frothy, lightweight stone light enough to float. The vesicles — gas cavities — can make up most of its volume. Pumice forms in explosive eruptions of silica-rich magma. It floats across oceans, carrying marine life, and its abrasive texture is used in polishing stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how trapped gas makes pumice so light, then explain why it floats on water.

name: Scoria
teaser: Scoria is dark, bubble-rich volcanic rock from gas-charged lava: unlike pumice, it's denser and sinks, with larger, rougher vesicles and a higher iron content. It forms in cinder cone eruptions where gas bubbles expand as lava cools. Scoria's rough texture makes it useful as lightweight aggregate in concrete and as landscaping rock. It's the froth of an eruption, preserved in stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how scoria forms from gas-filled lava, then explain the difference from pumice.

name: Andesite
teaser: Andesite is the volcanic rock of continental margins: medium-gray and intermediate in composition between basalt and rhyolite, it erupts at stratovolcanoes along subduction zones — the Andes gave it its name. It contains fine crystals of plagioclase, hornblende, and pyroxene. Andesitic lava is sticky and prone to explosive eruptions. It's the rock of the world's most dangerous volcanoes.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why andesite is named after the Andes, then explain its place at subduction zones.

name: Rhyolite
teaser: Rhyolite is the extrusive twin of granite: silica-rich, light-colored, and formed from thick, gas-rich lava that erupts explosively. Its rapid cooling gives it fine grains, sometimes with flow banding where the sticky lava folded as it moved. Rhyolite eruptions are among the most violent, producing calderas and ash flows. It's the continental crust's explosive export.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rhyolite forms from thick, gas-rich magma, then explain its explosive character.

name: Diorite
teaser: Diorite is an intermediate intrusive rock: coarser than andesite and lighter than gabbro, it's a mix of white plagioclase and dark hornblende, giving it a salt-and-pepper look. It forms in magma chambers where intermediate magma cools slowly. Diorite is tough and durable, used in ancient buildings and statues. Its composition sits between the crust's light granites and dark basalts.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how diorite forms between granite and gabbro, then explain its use in ancient statues.

name: Gabbro
teaser: Gabbro is the coarse-grained intrusive twin of basalt: dark, heavy, and rich in calcium feldspar and pyroxene, it cooled slowly in deep magma chambers. It forms the lower part of oceanic crust, beneath the basalt seafloor. Gabbro is dense and tough, used for crushed stone and countertops. Oceanic crust is essentially a basalt top over a gabbro base.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how gabbro forms slowly below the surface, then explain its link to the ocean crust.

name: Peridotite
teaser: Peridotite is the rock of Earth's mantle: dense, dark, and rich in olivine and pyroxene, it's what lies beneath the crust everywhere. It reaches the surface through tectonic windows and volcanic pipes, and its rare crystals — including diamond-bearing ones — come from deep mantle sources. Peridotite is the most abundant rock type on Earth, though the least seen.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why peridotite matters for the mantle, then explain how it reaches the surface.

name: Pegmatite
teaser: Pegmatite is an exceptionally coarse-grained igneous rock: it forms from water-rich magma that cools slowly in the last stages of crystallization, letting crystals grow to enormous sizes — some feldspar crystals are meters long. Pegmatites concentrate rare elements like lithium, beryllium, and tantalum, and they're a treasure house of gem minerals like tourmaline. One small pegmatite can yield museum-quality crystals.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how water-rich magma grows huge crystals, then explain why pegmatites yield gems.

name: Lava Tubes and Caves
teaser: Lava tubes form when the outer surface of a lava flow cools and hardens while the molten interior keeps flowing: the lava drains away, leaving a hollow tunnel. They can run for kilometers and are common in Hawaii and Iceland. Lava tubes are caves made by rivers of fire, and they can preserve the flow's shape perfectly. The same process may form tubes on the Moon and Mars.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how lava tubes form, then explain what lava stalactites are.

name: Igneous Textures
teaser: Igneous texture records cooling history: slow underground cooling grows large crystals — coarse texture; fast surface cooling grows small ones — fine texture; and instant chilling produces glass. Gas bubbles create vesicular texture, and mixed sizes — phenocrysts in fine groundmass — show two stages of cooling. Texture is the rock's cooling story, readable at a glance. Geologists read texture like a diary.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how grain size reveals cooling rate, then explain what porphyritic texture means.

name: Volcanic Glass
teaser: Volcanic glass forms when lava chills so fast that atoms can't arrange into crystals: obsidian is the classic, black and glassy, with a conchoidal fracture. Because it's not crystalline, it's technically an amorphous solid. Volcanic glass occurs where eruptions quench quickly, in lava, ash, and the edges of flows. It's the fastest cooling record in the igneous world.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how lava can freeze into glass, then explain what peperite and perlite are.

name: Igneous Landforms
teaser: Igneous landforms are the visible architecture of cooled magma: batholiths are vast underground granite bodies, sills and dikes are sheet-like intrusions, and laccoliths dome the surface. Extrusive forms include lava plateaus, domes, and volcanic cones. Erosion exposes the underground structures. From the granite domes of Yosemite to columnar basalt cliffs, these landforms reveal what magma built.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how magma shapes mountains and plateaus, then explain what a laccolith is.

name: Sedimentary Rocks
teaser: Sedimentary rocks form from accumulated particles: weathering breaks down older rock, water or wind carries the grains, and layers compact and cement into new rock — sandstone, shale, limestone. They cover most of the continents and preserve fossils, ripple marks, and the record of ancient environments. Most of what we know about Earth's history comes from sedimentary rocks. They're the archive of the rock cycle.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how sediment becomes rock over time, then explain why these rocks hold most fossils.

name: Weathering
teaser: Weathering breaks rock down in place: physical weathering fractures it through freeze-thaw, heat, and pressure changes, while chemical weathering dissolves and alters it — acid rain eating limestone, oxygen rusting iron minerals. Weathering produces soil, sediment, and the dissolved ions that rivers carry to the sea. It's the first step in the rock cycle, and it shapes nearly every landscape.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between physical and chemical weathering, then explain what frost wedging is.

name: Erosion
teaser: Erosion is the transport of weathered material: water, wind, ice, and gravity carry away sediment — rivers cut valleys, waves attack cliffs, glaciers grind mountains, and wind strips deserts. Erosion sculpts landscapes and delivers sediment to new resting places. It's the great leveler, wearing mountains down over millions of years. Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how water, wind and ice carry sediment, then explain the difference from weathering.

name: Deposition
teaser: Deposition is sediment coming to rest: when wind, water, or ice loses energy, the grains settle — rivers drop gravel where they slow, deltas build where rivers meet the sea, and wind piles dunes in deserts. Deposited layers become sedimentary rock through compaction and cementation. Deposition records environments: each site preserves a snapshot of where and how sediment landed.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why particles settle when currents slow, then explain what a delta is.

name: Lithification
teaser: Lithification turns loose sediment into rock: compaction squeezes grains together under the weight of overlying layers, and cementation glues them with minerals precipitating from groundwater — calcite, silica, iron oxide. Sand becomes sandstone, mud becomes shale. The process preserves sedimentary structures and fossils. Lithification is how the Earth archives its surface history.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how compaction and cementation bind grains, then explain what cement does.

name: Sandstone
teaser: Sandstone is sedimentary rock made of sand grains, usually quartz, cemented together: it forms where sand accumulates — beaches, deserts, riverbeds — and its grains and bedding record those environments. Cross-bedding shows ancient dune and current directions. Sandstone is porous, making it a key aquifer and oil reservoir rock. It's the rock of canyons like the Grand Canyon's red cliffs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sand becomes sandstone, then explain why it stores water and oil.

name: Shale
teaser: Shale is sedimentary rock made of compacted mud and clay: fine-grained and fissile, it splits into thin layers. It forms in quiet water — lakes, lagoons, deep seas — where fine particles settle slowly. Shale is the most common sedimentary rock, and it traps oil and gas within its layers. It's the source rock for many petroleum deposits and a fossil treasure house.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how mud compacts into shale, then explain why it is the most common sedimentary rock.

name: Limestone
teaser: Limestone is sedimentary rock made of calcium carbonate, mostly from the shells and skeletons of marine life: coral, shellfish, and microscopic plankton build it up layer by layer on the seafloor. It dissolves in acid, creating caves and karst landscapes, and it's the raw material of cement. Many limestones are pure fossil deposits. The rock itself is a graveyard of ancient seas.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how marine life builds limestone, then explain what chalk is.

name: Conglomerate
teaser: Conglomerate is sedimentary rock of rounded gravel: pebbles and cobbles rounded by tumbling in rivers or surf, cemented in sand or mud. The rounded clasts show they traveled — sharp edges were worn smooth. Conglomerate forms in high-energy environments like river channels and beaches. It's a record of fast-moving water and the debris it could carry.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rounded clasts become conglomerate, then explain the difference from breccia.

name: Breccia
teaser: Breccia is sedimentary rock of angular rock fragments: unlike conglomerate's rounded pebbles, breccia clasts are sharp-edged because they didn't travel far — the broken pieces were cemented where they fell. It forms at fault zones, rockfalls, and scree slopes. The angularity tells the story: short transport, violent origin. Breccia is the rock of sudden disruption.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how angular rubble becomes breccia, then explain where it typically forms.

name: Coal
teaser: Coal is sedimentary rock made of ancient plant matter: peat from swamps is buried, compacted, and heated over millions of years, progressively turning into lignite, bituminous coal, and finally anthracite. Each stage is richer in carbon and burns hotter. Coal formed in the Carboniferous's vast swamps and powered the Industrial Revolution. It's fossilized sunlight, stored in rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how plant matter becomes coal over millions of years, then explain the ranks from peat to anthracite.

name: Evaporites
teaser: Evaporites are minerals that precipitate as water evaporates: when seawater or lake water concentrates, calcite and gypsum deposit first, then halite (salt), and finally potassium and magnesium salts. Thick evaporite beds mark ancient dried-up seas and lakes. They're mined for salt, potash fertilizer, and gypsum. Evaporites are the Earth's salt cellars, recording vanished bodies of water.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how evaporation concentrates salts, then explain what rock salt is.

name: Chert
teaser: Chert is hard, fine-grained sedimentary rock made of microcrystalline quartz: it forms from the silica of tiny marine organisms like radiolarians and diatoms, or as nodules in limestone. It fractures conchoidally into razor edges, making it the first stone tool material — flint is a type of chert. Chert's hardness and edge-keeping made it humanity's earliest technology.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how chert forms from silica-rich water, then explain why flint was used for tools.

name: Dolomite
teaser: Dolomite is a carbonate rock and mineral — calcium magnesium carbonate: it resembles limestone but fizzes in acid only when powdered. It forms when magnesium-rich water alters limestone, or by direct precipitation. Dolomite is common in ancient rocks but rare in modern seas, a puzzle for geologists. It's used in construction, agriculture, and steelmaking.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how dolomite forms from limestone alteration, then explain the dolomite problem.

name: Sedimentary Structures
teaser: Sedimentary structures are the features frozen into rocks as they formed: ripple marks show flowing water, mud cracks show dried-up mud, cross-bedding shows dunes and currents, and graded bedding shows settling sediment. They record the environment and the energy of deposition. Geologists read these structures to reconstruct ancient landscapes. A bedding plane is a snapshot of the past.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what ripple marks and mud cracks record, then explain what cross-bedding is.

name: Ripple Marks
teaser: Ripple marks are the wavy ridges preserved on bedding surfaces when water or wind moved across sediment: symmetric ripples form from oscillating waves, asymmetric ones from currents flowing one way. Their spacing and shape record water depth and flow strength. Ripple marks on ancient rock prove the environment was once a shallow sea, river, or desert. They're frozen fingerprints of moving water.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how water and wind shape ripples, then explain what their direction reveals.

name: Mud Cracks
teaser: Mud cracks form when wet mud dries and shrinks, splitting into polygonal patterns: when later sediment fills the cracks and everything lithifies, the cracks are preserved as cast patterns on bedding surfaces. Mud cracks prove the sediment was exposed to air and dried — a shoreline or floodplain. They're simple but powerful evidence of ancient environments.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what mud cracks tell about ancient environments, then explain their polygonal shapes.

name: Fossil Fuels in Rock
teaser: Fossil fuels are stored in sedimentary rocks: oil and gas form from buried marine plankton that cooked under heat and pressure, then migrate into porous sandstone and limestone reservoirs trapped under impermeable layers. Coal forms from buried swamp vegetation. The chemistry of the source rock, reservoir, and seal decides where fuels accumulate. Sedimentary geology is the science of finding them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how source rocks and reservoirs trap oil, then explain what a reservoir rock is.

name: Sedimentary Basins
teaser: Sedimentary basins are low areas where sediment accumulates for millions of years: they form where the crust subsides — rift valleys, continental margins, and foreland basins in front of mountains. Thick basin fills can exceed ten kilometers, recording long environmental histories and hosting aquifers, oil, and coal. Basins are the great archives of Earth's surface, and they're where most economic deposits live.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how basins form and fill over time, then explain why they hold resources.

name: Sedimentary Environments
teaser: Sedimentary environments are the landscapes where sediment is deposited: rivers, deltas, beaches, deserts, reefs, and deep seas each leave a distinct signature of grain size, structures, and fossils. A river deposit is coarse and cross-bedded; a deep sea is fine mud with plankton fossils. Geologists match ancient rocks to modern environments to reconstruct past landscapes. Each environment writes its own kind of rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how deserts, rivers and reefs each leave distinct rocks, then explain what facies are.

name: Metamorphic Rocks
teaser: Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change existing rock without melting it: shale becomes slate, limestone becomes marble, and granite becomes gneiss as minerals recrystallize into new forms. The process happens deep in mountains, at plate boundaries, and around magma. Metamorphism preserves the rock's chemical identity while transforming its texture. It's the recycling of rock under extreme conditions.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how existing rocks change without melting, then explain what the name means.

name: Metamorphism
teaser: Metamorphism is the transformation of rock by heat, pressure, and chemically active fluids: existing minerals recrystallize, new minerals grow, and textures change — all without melting. Regional metamorphism accompanies mountain building over vast areas, while contact metamorphism cooks rock next to magma. The grade increases with temperature and pressure. Metamorphism is rock changing identity while staying solid.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what heat, pressure and fluids do to rocks, then explain the difference from melting.

name: Contact Metamorphism
teaser: Contact metamorphism cooks rock beside magma: the heat of an intrusion bakes the surrounding rock into a hard, fine-grained rock called hornfels, with new minerals like garnet forming in the hottest zone. The affected area is an aureole around the pluton, usually narrow. Pressure matters little here — heat is the agent. Contact metamorphism is a local oven baking the country rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how heat alone changes rocks, then explain what an aureole is.

name: Regional Metamorphism
teaser: Regional metamorphism transforms rock over huge areas during mountain building: the collision of plates buries rock to great depth, where heat and pressure recrystallize it over millions of years. The result is foliated rocks — slate, schist, gneiss — aligned with the mountain-building forces. Regional metamorphism affects whole belts, like the Appalachians or Alps. It's the largest-scale rock transformation on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how mountain building metamorphoses vast regions, then explain where it happens.

name: Foliation
teaser: Foliation is the layered, banded texture of metamorphic rock: flat minerals like mica align perpendicular to pressure, stacking into sheets — the rock splits along them. Higher grade produces coarser foliation: slate's fine cleavage, schist's shiny flakes, gneiss's distinct bands. Foliation records the direction and intensity of the forces that deformed the rock. It's pressure made visible in stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why pressure aligns minerals into bands, then explain what schistosity is.

name: Slate
teaser: Slate is the low-grade metamorphic rock of mudstone and shale: heat and pressure recrystallize the clay into microscopic mica flakes aligned in parallel, giving slate its perfect cleavage into thin sheets. It's hard, fine-grained, and splits cleanly, which is why it's used for roofing and chalkboards. Slate forms early in metamorphism, before larger crystals grow. It's the first step up the metamorphic grade.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how shale becomes slate, then explain why it splits into thin sheets.

name: Schist
teaser: Schist is a medium-grade metamorphic rock with visible mica flakes: the aligned sheets of mica, chlorite, or graphite give it a shiny, layered look and a tendency to split. It forms where regional metamorphism recrystallizes shale or basalt under moderate heat and pressure. Schist often contains garnet, staurolite, or kyanite crystals. It's a rock of visible transformation — the minerals are large enough to see.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how slate becomes schist, then explain what its glitter comes from.

name: Gneiss
teaser: Gneiss is a high-grade metamorphic rock with distinct light and dark bands: at high temperature and pressure, minerals separate into layers — quartz and feldspar in light bands, mica and amphibole in dark ones. It forms from granite or sedimentary rocks deeply buried in mountain belts. The banding can be folded and contorted by continued deformation. Gneiss is metamorphism pushed to its visual extreme.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how schist becomes gneiss, then explain what its bands reveal.

name: Marble
teaser: Marble is limestone transformed by heat and pressure: calcite crystals recrystallize and grow, turning the rock into a dense, interlocking mass that polishes beautifully. Pure limestone gives white marble; impurities add colors and veins. Marble has been the sculptor's stone since ancient Greece — Michelangelo's David is marble. It's metamorphosed shell and coral, hardened into art.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how limestone becomes marble, then explain why sculptors love it.

name: Quartzite
teaser: Quartzite is sandstone that metamorphosed: heat and pressure recrystallize the quartz grains, fusing them together so the rock breaks through the grains, not around them. It's extremely hard and resistant, forming ridgelines where softer rock erodes away. Pure quartzite is white or pink; iron impurities add red. Quartzite is the metamorphic armor of mountain ranges.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sandstone becomes quartzite, then explain why it breaks through sandstone.

name: Hornfels
teaser: Hornfels is the baked rock of contact metamorphism: fine-grained, hard, and dark, it forms when magma heats shale or other rock intensely without deforming it. The clay minerals recrystallize into a dense mosaic — no foliation, just a tough, splintery rock. Hornfels can contain new minerals like cordierite and garnet near the heat source. It's the signature product of rock cooked in place.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how contact metamorphism makes hornfels, then explain why it is so tough.

name: Amphibolite
teaser: Amphibolite is a medium-to-high-grade metamorphic rock rich in amphibole minerals like hornblende: it forms from basalt or gabbro metamorphosed under moderate heat and pressure, usually in mountain belts. Dark hornblende and white plagioclase give it a banded or blocky look. Amphibolite is common in old continental crust. It's the metamorphic form of the ocean floor's basalt.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how basalts metamorphose into amphibolite, then explain its place in mountain belts.

name: Eclogite
teaser: Eclogite is a high-pressure metamorphic rock formed deep in subduction zones: basaltic rock recrystallizes into bright green omphacite and red garnet at depths of 50 kilometers or more. Eclogite is dense — denser than the mantle around it — and its presence marks where old ocean crust was dragged down. Some eclogites return to the surface as evidence of deep subduction. It's metamorphism at the planet's limits.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how eclogite forms in subduction zones, then explain its surprising density.

name: Metamorphic Grade
teaser: Metamorphic grade measures how intense the heat and pressure were: low grade — slate and phyllite — forms at shallow depths and modest temperatures, while high grade — gneiss and migmatite — requires deep burial and near-melting heat. Each grade produces characteristic minerals and textures. Grade is the metamorphic thermometer and barometer combined. Geologists read a rock's grade to reconstruct its burial history.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how grade increases from slate to gneiss, then explain what index minerals are.

name: Index Minerals
teaser: Index minerals mark metamorphic grade: chlorite appears at low grade, garnet at medium, and sillimanite at high, each forming at a specific temperature and pressure. Their presence pins the rock's metamorphic conditions. Found in a region, index minerals map the metamorphic zones radiating from a heat source. They're the geologist's temperature gauges, frozen in stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how certain minerals mark metamorphic zones, then explain why garnet is an index mineral.

name: Migmatite
teaser: Migmatite is the twilight zone of metamorphism: a mixed rock where part melted and part didn't, showing light igneous veins cutting through dark metamorphic rock. It forms at the highest grade, where temperatures approach the melting point — partial melting begins and the melt veins freeze in place. Migmatite marks the transition between metamorphism and full melting. It's rock caught mid-transformation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how migmatite forms at the edge of melting, then explain what partial melting means.

name: Shock Metamorphism
teaser: Shock metamorphism is transformation by impact: when a meteorite slams into Earth, the shock wave subjects rock to pressures and temperatures far beyond normal metamorphism in an instant. Minerals deform in unique ways — quartz develops planar fractures called shock lamellae, and rock melts into glass. Shock features are the fingerprint of asteroid impacts, preserved in impact craters worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how meteorite impacts transform rock, then explain what impact breccia is.

name: Metamorphic Textures
teaser: Metamorphic textures record the conditions of transformation: foliated textures show aligned minerals under directed pressure, while non-foliated textures — like marble's interlocking calcite — grow under uniform stress. Grain size increases with grade, and porphyroblasts are large crystals that grew during metamorphism. Texture reveals whether the rock was squeezed, baked, or both.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how grain size and foliation reflect conditions, then explain what porphyroblasts are.

name: Metamorphic Facies
teaser: Metamorphic facies are sets of minerals that form under specific pressure-temperature conditions: greenschist facies marks low-grade metamorphism, amphibolite facies moderate, and eclogite facies the high-pressure deep-subduction zone. Each facies is defined by a characteristic mineral assemblage. Finding a facies tells geologists the depth and temperature a rock reached. Facies are metamorphism's coordinate system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how facies map the conditions of metamorphism, then explain what blueschist marks.

name: Metamorphic Paths
teaser: A metamorphic path is the journey a rock takes through pressure and temperature over time: burial and heating on the way down, uplift and cooling on the way back. Minerals that grow at each stage record the route — some rocks even preserve different minerals from different parts of their path. Geologists reconstruct these paths to understand mountain building and subduction. A metamorphic rock is a travel log.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rocks record changing conditions as they move, then explain what retrograde metamorphism is.

name: Plate Tectonics
teaser: Plate tectonics is the unifying theory of geology: Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move on the hot, ductile mantle below. Where plates diverge, new crust forms; where they converge, crust subducts or collides; where they slide past, faults grind. Plate motions drive earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building. The theory, confirmed in the 1960s, explains how the Earth works as a system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Earth's outer shell splits into moving plates, then explain why the theory transformed geology.

name: Continental Drift
teaser: Continental drift was Alfred Wegener's 1912 idea that continents move: he noticed matching coastlines, identical fossils, and similar rock sequences across oceans, and proposed a single supercontinent, Pangaea. He lacked a mechanism, and geologists rejected it for decades. The theory was vindicated when seafloor spreading and plate tectonics provided the engine. Wegener was right about the fact, wrong only about the timing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Wegener proposed moving continents, then explain why his idea was rejected at first.

name: Pangaea
teaser: Pangaea was the supercontinent that existed about 300-200 million years ago: all of today's continents were joined in a single landmass, surrounded by one ocean, Panthalassa. Pangaea assembled from older continents and later rifted apart — its breakup produced the Atlantic Ocean. Fossil and rock matches across continents were the first clues. Pangaea explains why similar fossils appear on different shores.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how all land once formed Pangaea, then explain what fossils prove it.

name: Seafloor Spreading
teaser: Seafloor spreading is the engine of continental drift: magma rises at mid-ocean ridges, forming new oceanic crust that pushes outward on both sides. The seafloor grows, and the Atlantic widens by a few centimeters a year. Harry Hess proposed it in 1960, and magnetic stripes on the seafloor confirmed it. Seafloor spreading explains how continents ride the spreading ocean crust.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges, then explain what magnetic stripes reveal.

name: Evidence for Drift
teaser: The evidence for continental drift is everywhere in the rock record: matching coastlines, identical fossils and rock types on different continents, paleoclimate clues like glacial deposits in now-tropical places, and the magnetic stripes of the seafloor. Together they show the continents once formed one landmass and drifted apart. Wegener assembled the clues; plate tectonics supplied the mechanism.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how matching coastlines, fossils and rocks support drift, then explain why glacial evidence matters.

name: Plate Boundaries
teaser: Plate boundaries are where Earth's tectonic plates interact, and they come in three types: divergent boundaries pull apart, creating new crust; convergent boundaries collide, subducting or building mountains; and transform boundaries slide past each other. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur at boundaries. The boundary type determines the geology: rifts, trenches, island arcs, and fault zones. Plate interactions build the planet's surface features.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the three boundary types, then explain what happens where plates collide.

name: Divergent Boundaries
teaser: Divergent boundaries are where plates pull apart: magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust — mid-ocean ridges under the sea and rift valleys on land. The Atlantic grows at its ridge; East Africa rifts apart. Earthquakes are shallow and volcanoes gentle. Divergent boundaries are the Earth's conveyor belt, continuously manufacturing new ocean floor.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rifts and ridges open, then explain what forms when plates split.

name: Convergent Boundaries
teaser: Convergent boundaries are where plates collide: dense oceanic crust subducts beneath lighter crust, melting and feeding explosive volcanoes, while continental collisions crush rock into mountain belts. Oceanic-continental convergence builds the Andes; continental-continental convergence builds the Himalayas. Subduction produces deep trenches, intense earthquakes, and arc volcanoes. Convergent boundaries are the Earth's most violent plate interactions.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what happens when plates collide, then explain the three kinds of convergence.

name: Transform Boundaries
teaser: Transform boundaries are where plates slide horizontally past each other: crust is neither created nor destroyed, but friction builds and releases as earthquakes — the San Andreas Fault is the classic. The offsets are visible in rivers, ridges, and fence lines displaced by quakes. Transform faults connect other boundary segments. They're the Earth's grinding, sticking, and slipping plate edges.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how plates slide sideways, then explain what the San Andreas fault is.

name: Subduction
teaser: Subduction is the descent of one tectonic plate beneath another: dense oceanic crust dives into the mantle at a trench, carrying sediment and water with it. The sinking plate triggers earthquakes to great depth, and the water and heat melt the overlying mantle, feeding arc volcanoes. Subduction recycles oceanic crust back into the mantle. It's the engine of the deepest earthquakes and most explosive volcanoes.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how dense plates sink into the mantle, then explain what a subduction zone is.

name: Subduction Zones
teaser: Subduction zones are where one plate dives beneath another: marked by deep ocean trenches, they produce the world's largest earthquakes, explosive volcanic arcs, and mountain building. The subducting slab carries water down, which melts the mantle above and feeds the volcanoes — Japan, the Andes, and the Cascades all sit on subduction zones. The Pacific Ring of Fire is a chain of subduction zones.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why subduction zones produce the deepest quakes, then explain what a Wadati-Benioff zone is.

name: Mid-Ocean Ridges
teaser: Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountain chains where plates diverge and new crust forms: magma rises along the ridge, cools into basalt, and pushes the plates apart — the longest mountain system on Earth, stretching 65,000 kilometers. The ridges are marked by shallow earthquakes, hydrothermal vents, and volcanic activity. Iceland is the ridge rising above the sea. The mid-ocean ridge is the Earth's crust factory.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ridges run through every ocean, then explain why they matter for crust formation.

name: Ocean Trenches
teaser: Ocean trenches are the deepest places on Earth, where plates subduct: the Mariana Trench plunges nearly 11 kilometers, deeper than Everest is tall. Trenches mark the surface expression of subduction, with the bending plate forming a deep groove. They host unique life around hydrothermal vents and capture the sediment scraped off subducting plates. Trenches are the Earth's deep scars of plate consumption.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how trenches form at subduction zones, then explain why they are the deepest places on Earth.

name: Rift Valleys
teaser: Rift valleys form where continental crust pulls apart: the crust stretches, cracks into faults, and the block between drops — the East African Rift and the Basin and Range are examples. Rifts fill with sediment and lakes, and volcanoes line the fault margins. If rifting continues, the continent splits and an ocean forms. A rift valley is a continent in the middle of divorcing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rifts form and widen, then explain what the East African Rift is.

name: Continental Collision
teaser: Continental collision happens when two continents converge: neither subducts easily — both are buoyant — so the crust thickens, crumples, and rises into mountain belts. The Himalayas formed when India slammed into Asia, and the Alps from Africa colliding with Europe. Collision zones have the thickest crust on Earth and intense deformation. The rock record shows ancient collisions in nearly every continent's core.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Himalayas formed, then explain why continental crust does not subduct easily.

name: Island Arcs
teaser: Island arcs are chains of volcanoes where oceanic plates subduct beneath other oceanic plates: the subducting slab melts the mantle, feeding volcanic islands in a curved line — Japan, the Aleutians, Indonesia. Behind the arc, back-arc basins may open. Island arcs grow into continents over time, adding new crust. They're the volcanic signature of ocean-ocean subduction.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how volcanic arcs form at subduction zones, then explain why they curve.

name: Mantle Hotspots
teaser: Mantle hotspots are stationary plumes of hot rock rising from deep in the mantle: as a plate moves over a hotspot, the plume punches through, creating a chain of volcanoes — the Hawaiian-Emperor chain records 80 million years of plate motion. Hotspots build islands, feed supervolcanoes like Yellowstone, and occur far from plate boundaries. They're the Earth's fixed reference points for plate motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hotspots create volcanic chains, then explain what the Hawaiian chain shows.

name: How Fast Plates Move
teaser: Tectonic plates move a few centimeters per year — about the speed fingernails grow: the Atlantic widens 2-4 cm a year, the Pacific plate moves 7-10 cm. Over millions of years, that slow crawl moves continents across oceans. GPS satellites now measure the motion directly, millimeter by millimeter. Plate speed is slow in human terms, but unstoppable in geologic ones.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fast plates actually move, then explain how GPS measures them.

name: Paleomagnetism
teaser: Paleomagnetism studies the magnetic record frozen in rocks: iron minerals align with Earth's magnetic field when rocks form, and they keep that alignment — recording the field's direction and polarity at the time. Magnetic stripes on the seafloor, alternating normally and reversed, proved seafloor spreading. Paleomagnetism also tracks continental drift and magnetic reversals. It's the compass reading of ancient rocks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rocks record ancient magnetism, then explain how it proved seafloor spreading.

name: The Future Supercontinent
teaser: The continents are still moving, and they're converging into a new supercontinent: projections suggest Pangaea Ultima or Amasia will form in 200-300 million years as the Atlantic closes. The Mediterranean will vanish as Africa and Europe merge, and the Pacific may shrink. Earth's future face is being sketched by the plate motions measured today. Deep-time forecast: the next Pangaea is on its way.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how current plate motion may form a new supercontinent, then explain what Pangaea Ultima is.

name: Earth's Layered Structure
teaser: Earth is layered like an onion: a thin crust of rock, a thick mantle of hot silicate, a liquid outer core of iron, and a solid inner core. The layers differ in composition and state — crust and mantle are rock, core is metal. Seismic waves reveal the boundaries. Each layer's chemistry and physics drive the surface geology we see. Earth's structure is the deep engine of everything at the surface.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how scientists know Earth's layers, then explain why seismic waves are the key.

name: The Crust
teaser: The crust is Earth's thin outer shell: oceanic crust is about 7 kilometers of dense basalt, while continental crust averages 35 kilometers of lighter granite-rich rock. The crust floats on the mantle, and it's where all life, rocks, and human activity exist. It's continuously created at ridges and recycled at subduction zones. The crust is a thin skin — proportionally thinner than an eggshell.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the crust is made of, then explain the difference between oceanic and continental crust.

name: The Mantle
teaser: The mantle is Earth's 2,900-kilometer-thick layer of hot silicate rock: it's solid but flows extremely slowly, carrying heat by convection. Mantle convection drives plate tectonics, and mantle plumes build hotspots. Although almost never seen, mantle rock reaches the surface as peridotite and basalt. The mantle holds most of Earth's volume and heat. It's the slow, churning engine beneath the crust.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why the mantle flows over long times, then explain what mantle convection is.

name: The Core
teaser: The core is Earth's metallic heart: a ball of iron and nickel about 3,500 kilometers in radius. The outer core is liquid and churns, generating the magnetic field through a dynamo effect; the inner core is solid iron, as hot as the sun's surface. The core formed early, as heavy metals sank. It drives the magnetic shield that protects the atmosphere from solar wind.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the core formed, then explain the difference between inner and outer core.

name: The Inner Core
teaser: The inner core is a solid ball of iron-nickel about 1,220 kilometers in radius, despite temperatures near 5,000°C — the pressure is so immense that the metal stays solid. It's slowly growing as the outer core freezes onto it, releasing heat that drives convection. Seismic waves revealed its existence in 1936. The inner core may even rotate at a slightly different rate than the rest of the planet.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why the inner core is solid despite the heat, then explain what keeps it that way.

name: The Outer Core
teaser: The outer core is a liquid layer of molten iron-nickel about 2,200 kilometers thick: its churning motion, driven by heat and Earth's rotation, generates the magnetic field through the dynamo effect. The field extends into space, deflecting solar wind and protecting the atmosphere. The liquid metal also conducts electricity, which is essential to the dynamo. The outer core is the planet's liquid-metal generator.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the outer core generates the magnetic field, then explain why it is liquid.

name: The Lithosphere
teaser: The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell: the crust plus the uppermost mantle, about 100 kilometers thick, broken into the tectonic plates. It's strong and cool enough to behave elastically, bending and breaking rather than flowing. The lithosphere floats on the weaker asthenosphere below. Plate tectonics is the motion of lithosphere. It's the shell that carries continents and oceans.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what makes up the lithosphere, then explain how it differs from the asthenosphere.

name: The Asthenosphere
teaser: The asthenosphere is the soft, ductile layer of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere: heat and pressure make it behave like slow, weak plastic that can flow over geologic time. The rigid plates ride on this flowing layer, and its convection drives their motion. Seismic waves slow in the asthenosphere, revealing its partially molten state. It's the conveyor belt beneath the moving plates.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the asthenosphere is weak and ductile, then explain how plates move over it.

name: Earth's Magnetic Field
teaser: Earth's magnetic field is generated by the dynamo of the liquid outer core: churning molten iron creates electric currents that produce the field, which extends far into space. The field deflects the solar wind and cosmic rays, shielding the atmosphere and life from radiation. Compasses align to it, and animals navigate by it. The field also flips polarity occasionally — reversals recorded in rocks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the dynamo creates the field, then explain why the poles wander.

name: Magnetic Reversals
teaser: Magnetic reversals are flips in Earth's magnetic polarity: the north and south magnetic poles trade places, as recorded by iron minerals aligning in cooling rocks. Reversals happen irregularly, roughly every few hundred thousand years, and the last one was about 780,000 years ago. Magnetic stripes on the seafloor — alternating normal and reversed — proved seafloor spreading. The field has flipped hundreds of times in Earth's history.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Earth's poles flip over time, then explain what the record in rocks shows.

name: Earth's Internal Heat
teaser: Earth's internal heat comes from two sources: primordial heat left from formation and radioactive decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the mantle and crust. The heat flows outward, driving mantle convection, plate tectonics, and volcanism. The geotherm — temperature increasing with depth — reaches about 5,000°C at the center. Earth's heat is slowly cooling, and its budget sets the pace of geologic activity.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where Earth's heat comes from, then explain the role of radioactive decay.

name: Seismic Waves
teaser: Seismic waves are vibrations that travel through Earth from earthquakes, explosions, or impacts: they're the planet's natural X-rays. Body waves — P and S — travel through the interior, while surface waves roll along the top and cause most damage. Seismic waves bend and reflect at layer boundaries, revealing Earth's structure. Seismologists read them like ultrasound images of the planet's interior.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how P and S waves travel, then explain what the shadow zone reveals.

name: P Waves
teaser: P waves — primary waves — are the fastest seismic waves: they compress and expand material like sound waves, traveling through solids, liquids, and gases. They arrive first at seismometers, hence the name. P waves can pass through the core, which let geologists map its boundaries. Their speed varies with the material, revealing composition and temperature. P waves are the first messengers of an earthquake.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how compression waves travel through solids and liquids, then explain what P stands for.

name: S Waves
teaser: S waves — secondary waves — are slower seismic waves that shake material perpendicular to their travel: they can't pass through liquids, which is why they stop at the outer core — a key clue that it's molten. S waves arrive after P waves and cause much of the damaging shaking in an earthquake. Their behavior maps the solid and liquid layers of the deep Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why S waves cannot pass through liquids, then explain what this told scientists about the core.

name: Seismic Tomography
teaser: Seismic tomography is like a CT scan of Earth: thousands of seismic waves from earthquakes are combined by computers to image the planet's interior in three dimensions. The images reveal cold subducting slabs sinking into the mantle, hot plumes rising, and the boundaries between layers. Tomography showed that plates descend deep and mantle plumes rise from the core-mantle boundary. It's the modern window into the deep Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how scientists image the mantle like a CT scan, then explain what hot and cold blobs reveal.

name: The Age of Earth
teaser: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, determined by radiometric dating: the oldest Earth minerals — zircon crystals from Australia — date to 4.4 billion years, and meteorites, which formed with the solar system, give the same age. The age was debated for centuries — Lord Kelvin estimated tens of millions — until radioactivity provided the clock. Earth is nearly as old as the solar system itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Earth's age was determined, then explain the role of meteorites and lead isotopes.

name: How Earth Formed
teaser: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the solar nebula: dust and gas clumped into planetesimals that collided and merged, growing by accretion into a planet. The collisions released enormous heat, melting Earth into a molten sphere whose heavy metals sank to form the core. The surface cooled into crust, oceans condensed from steam, and the Moon formed from a giant impact. The young Earth was a violent place.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the solar nebula built Earth, then explain what accretion is.

name: How the Moon Formed
teaser: The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago from a giant impact: a Mars-sized body crashed into the young Earth, and the debris blasted into orbit coalesced into the Moon. The evidence is chemical — the Moon's rocks are nearly identical to Earth's mantle, and its iron-poor composition matches a crust-stripped impact. The Moon stabilizes Earth's tilt, driving tides and stabilizing the seasons.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a Mars-sized impact may have made the Moon, then explain what the evidence is.

name: Earth's Density
teaser: Earth's average density is 5.5 grams per cubic centimeter — far denser than surface rocks — because the interior is metal: the iron-nickel core is dense, while crustal rocks are light. The density increases with depth, revealed by gravity and seismic waves. The dense core and light crust are the result of differentiation — heavy material sank early in Earth's history. Density is the organizing principle of Earth's layers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how average density reveals the iron core, then explain how it was measured.

name: Gravity Mapping
teaser: Gravity mapping measures tiny variations in Earth's gravitational pull: dense rock below — ore bodies, mantle upwellings — pulls harder, while sediment-filled basins pull less. Satellites map these anomalies from orbit, and ground gravimeters add detail. Gravity surveys find mineral deposits, map crustal thickness, and track groundwater and ice changes. The Earth's gravity field is a map of its hidden structure.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how satellites map gravity variations, then explain what a geoid is.

name: Volcanoes
teaser: Volcanoes are vents where magma reaches the surface: when plates diverge, subduct, or pass over hotspots, mantle rock melts and rises, erupting lava, ash, and gas. Volcanoes build mountains, islands, and new crust, and their eruptions range from gentle lava flows to explosive blasts. They're Earth's way of releasing internal heat. Volcanoes are both destructive and creative — they build the land we live on.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what a volcano is and how it erupts, then explain the difference between magma and lava.

name: Volcanic Eruptions
teaser: Volcanic eruptions range from quiet lava fountains to cataclysmic explosions, controlled by the magma's gas content and viscosity: runny basaltic magma releases gas gently, while thick, silica-rich magma traps gas until pressure blasts it out. Eruptions produce lava, ash, pyroclastic flows, and lahars. They shape landscapes, create new land, and occasionally alter climate. Every eruption is a release of Earth's internal pressure.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what drives an eruption, then explain the role of dissolved gas.

name: Shield Volcanoes
teaser: Shield volcanoes are broad, gently sloping mountains built by runny basaltic lava: each eruption spreads thin lava far, stacking wide, shallow layers — Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea in Hawaii, and Olympus Mons on Mars are classic shields. Their eruptions are usually non-explosive. Shield volcanoes are the largest volcanoes on Earth by volume. They're the product of low-viscosity magma flowing freely.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why shield volcanoes are wide and flat, then explain what Hawaii shows.

name: Stratovolcanoes
teaser: Stratovolcanoes are the steep, cone-shaped volcanoes of subduction zones: alternating layers of lava and ash build their slopes — Fuji, Vesuvius, and Mount St. Helens are examples. Their magma is viscous and gas-rich, making eruptions explosive and dangerous. Stratovolcanoes produce pyroclastic flows, lahars, and ash falls. They're the classic volcano shape and the most hazardous type.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why composite cones alternate lava and ash, then explain why they are dangerous.

name: Cinder Cones
teaser: Cinder cones are the smallest volcanoes: steep-sided hills built from frothy lava fragments — cinders — ejected by gas-charged eruptions. The fragments fall around the vent, building a cone with a crater at the top. Most cinder cones erupt once, like Arizona's Sunset Crater. They're the most common volcano type on Earth, often forming in clusters on larger volcanoes' flanks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how cinder cones form from one eruption, then explain what cinders are.

name: Calderas
teaser: A caldera is a large volcanic depression formed when a volcano's magma chamber empties and the ground collapses: the 1980 Mount St. Helens blast and Yellowstone's vast caldera are examples. Some calderas fill with water, like Crater Lake, or continue erupting inside, like Santorini. Caldera-forming eruptions are among the most violent on Earth. The collapse marks where a volcano's foundation gave way.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how calderas form when magma chambers empty, then explain what Yellowstone is.

name: Lava Flows
teaser: Lava flows are rivers of molten rock moving across the surface: runny basaltic flows travel fast and far, building shield volcanoes, while thick, sticky flows crawl and mound. As lava cools, it crusts — pahoehoe forms smooth ropey surfaces, and aa forms jagged blocky ones. Lava flows destroy everything in their path but create new land. They're the most visible form of volcanic eruption.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the types of lava flows, then explain the difference between pahoehoe and aa.

name: Pyroclastic Flows
