teaser: Pyroclastic flows are avalanches of hot gas, ash, and rock racing down volcano slopes: they travel hundreds of kilometers per hour at temperatures exceeding 500°C, hugging the ground like a fluid. They're the deadliest volcanic hazard — Pompeii was buried by one, and they leveled whole towns at Mount St. Helens. Pyroclastic flows form when eruption columns collapse. There is no outrunning them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fast pyroclastic flows travel, then explain what killed the people of Pompeii.

name: Volcanic Ash
teaser: Volcanic ash is fine rock and glass fragments blasted from eruptions: particles range from dust to pebbles, and they're sharp, abrasive, and can travel thousands of kilometers on wind. Ash collapses roofs, chokes engines, and contaminates water, and its glass shards damage lungs. In the stratosphere, fine ash and gas reflect sunlight and can cool the climate. Ash is the eruption's far-reaching arm.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how eruptions loft ash into the sky, then explain the difference from lava.

name: Lahars
teaser: Lahars are volcanic mudflows: volcanic ash and debris mixed with water — from melted snow, heavy rain, or crater lakes — rush down valleys at highway speeds. They bury everything in mud, like the 1985 Armero disaster in Colombia that killed 23,000 people. Lahars can occur long after an eruption ends. They're among the most deadly volcanic hazards because they travel far beyond the volcano.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ash and water create deadly mudflows, then explain why lahars can arrive without eruption.

name: Volcanic Gases
teaser: Volcanoes release gases — mostly water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide, with smaller amounts of hydrogen sulfide and halogens: the gas drives eruption explosivity, and its composition signals magma movement. Sulfur dioxide reaches the stratosphere and cools climate, as Pinatubo's 1991 eruption showed. CO2 can accumulate in low areas and suffocate. Volcanic gas is both a hazard and a monitoring tool — rising gas warns of eruptions.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what gases volcanoes release, then explain why CO2 can pool in valleys.

name: Volcanic Bombs
teaser: Volcanic bombs are molten rock fragments thrown from erupting vents: they cool into aerodynamic shapes — spindle, bread-crust, or ribbon forms — as they spin through the air. Bombs range from fist-sized to car-sized and land with force, cratering the ground. They're solid evidence of an eruption's violence. Bombs cool fast, preserving their shapes as geological signatures.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how blobs of lava become bombs in the air, then explain their spindle shapes.

name: Vesuvius
teaser: Vesuvius is the famous volcano that buried Pompeii in 79 CE: the eruption blasted ash and pyroclastic flows over the Roman cities, preserving them for 1,700 years under meters of debris. Vesuvius is still active, looming over Naples, and its past violence makes it one of the most closely monitored volcanoes on Earth. The disaster gave science its first detailed eruption account — Pliny the Younger's letters.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the 79 CE eruption that destroyed Roman cities, then explain why it still threatens Naples.

name: Krakatoa
teaser: Krakatoa's 1883 eruption was one of history's loudest events: the Indonesian volcano exploded, collapsing into the sea and generating tsunamis that killed tens of thousands. The blast was heard 4,800 kilometers away, and ash circled the globe, dimming sunsets for years. A new cone, Anak Krakatoa, has grown in the caldera since. Krakatoa showed how a single eruption can affect the whole planet.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the 1883 eruption shook the globe, then explain what the tsunami did.

name: Mount St. Helens
teaser: Mount St. Helens erupted on May 18, 1980, in the first major eruption in the contiguous US in over a century: a massive landslide uncorked the volcano, triggering a lateral blast that flattened forests for 600 square kilometers and sent ash across the country. Fifty-seven people died. The eruption devastated the landscape but became a living laboratory for ecosystem recovery. It reshaped how America monitors volcanoes.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the 1980 eruption blew sideways, then explain what bulge warned of it.

name: Ring of Fire
teaser: The Ring of Fire is the belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean: subduction zones circle the Pacific — from the Andes to Japan to the Aleutians — producing most of Earth's active volcanoes and largest earthquakes. About 75% of the world's volcanoes and 90% of its earthquakes occur here. The Ring of Fire is the visible edge of the Pacific plate being consumed. It's the most geologically active region on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the Pacific rim is so volcanically active, then explain its connection to subduction.

name: Volcano Monitoring
teaser: Volcano monitoring watches the warning signs of eruption: seismometers track the earthquakes of moving magma, GPS measures ground swelling, gas sensors detect rising sulfur dioxide, and satellites spot heat and ash. Rising magma causes measurable changes — often for days or weeks before an eruption. Monitoring let scientists predict Mount Pinatubo's 1991 blast and save thousands of lives. Watching a volcano's chemistry and physics gives early warning.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how scientists predict eruptions, then explain what deformation means.

name: Supervolcanoes
teaser: Supervolcanoes are volcanoes capable of eruptions thousands of times larger than normal: they're fed by huge magma chambers and erupt through massive calderas — Yellowstone is the famous example. A supereruption would blanket continents in ash and cool global climate for years. The last occurred 26,000 years ago, and the next is unpredictable, but monitoring shows no imminent threat. Supervolcanoes are Earth's largest, rarest, most destructive eruptions.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what makes a supervolcano, then explain how big the last Yellowstone eruption was.

name: The Life of a Volcano
teaser: Volcanoes have life cycles spanning hundreds of thousands of years: they grow through repeated eruptions, reach a peak, and eventually go dormant as magma supply shifts. Individual eruptions last days to decades; the volcano's active phase lasts far longer. Erosion eventually dismantles the cone. Dormant volcanoes can reawaken after centuries — Vesuvius slept for 500 years before Pompeii. A volcano's life is long, but not eternal.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how volcanoes grow and die, then explain the difference between dormant and extinct.

name: Volcanoes Beyond Earth
teaser: Volcanoes exist throughout the solar system: Mars has Olympus Mons, the largest volcano known; Jupiter's moon Io erupts constantly with sulfur; Venus may have active lava flows; and icy moons like Enceladus erupt water. Each world's volcanism runs on different chemistry — rock, ice, or sulfur. Studying them shows volcanism is a universal planetary process. Earth is not the only volcanic world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn where else in the solar system volcanoes exist, then explain what Olympus Mons is.

name: Types of Faults
teaser: Faults are fractures where rock has moved, and they come in types based on motion: normal faults drop one block down along a dipping plane, reverse and thrust faults push one block up, and strike-slip faults slide blocks past each other horizontally. The motion reflects the stress — pulling apart, squeezing, or shearing. Fault type tells geologists the forces that shaped a region. Every fault records a direction of strain.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the three main fault types, then explain what the hanging wall is.

name: Normal Faults
teaser: Normal faults form where crust stretches and pulls apart: the hanging wall slides down the fault plane, dropping one block below another. They create rift valleys, basin-and-range landscapes, and stepped escarpments. Earthquakes on normal faults are usually moderate. Normal faults are the signature of extension — regions where the crust is being thinned.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how extension creates normal faults, then explain what a footwall is.

name: Reverse Faults
teaser: Reverse faults form where crust is squeezed: the hanging wall pushes up over the footwall along a steep fault plane, shortening the crust. When the plane is shallow, they're called thrust faults. Reverse faults build mountain ranges and thicken the crust in collision zones. Their earthquakes can be powerful. Reverse faults are the signature of compression — regions where plates are colliding.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how compression makes reverse faults, then explain what a thrust fault is.

name: Strike-Slip Faults
teaser: Strike-slip faults slide rock horizontally past each other: the San Andreas Fault is the most famous, where the Pacific and North American plates grind sideways. Motion along the fault offsets rivers, fences, and roads over time. Strike-slip faults produce some of the largest earthquakes — the 1906 San Francisco quake moved the ground meters. They're the signature of plates shearing past each other.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how lateral motion creates strike-slip faults, then explain the difference between right and left lateral.

name: Oblique Faults
teaser: Oblique faults combine two kinds of motion: rock slides both vertically and horizontally along the fault plane — a mix of normal or reverse and strike-slip. They form where stress arrives at an angle rather than perfectly head-on. Oblique faults are common at plate boundaries with complex geometry. Their mixed motion makes them harder to characterize, but they're the norm in many fault systems.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how oblique motion combines slip styles, then explain where they occur.

name: The San Andreas Fault
teaser: The San Andreas Fault is the transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates: it runs 1,300 kilometers through California, sliding at a few centimeters a year. The fault is famous for the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the constant threat of the next big one. It offsets rivers and ridges, and its creeping segments move silently while locked ones build stress. The fault defines California's earthquake risk.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the San Andreas works, then explain the cities it threatens.

name: Fault Lines
teaser: Fault lines are the surface traces of faults: the line where a fault plane meets the ground, often marked by scarps, offset streams, and linear valleys. Fault lines aren't single cracks — they're zones of fractured rock that can be kilometers wide. Mapping them shows where future earthquakes are likely. Fault lines shape topography and, increasingly, determine where cities plan and build.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what fault lines look like at the surface, then explain why maps show them.

name: Fault Rupture
teaser: Fault rupture is the sudden slip that causes an earthquake: stress builds for decades or centuries, then the fault breaks along a segment — sometimes hundreds of kilometers — releasing the stored energy as seismic waves. The 1906 San Francisco quake ruptured 430 kilometers of the San Andreas in seconds. Rupture can also break the surface, offsetting roads and fences. The length and slip of a rupture set the earthquake's size.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how quakes split the surface, then explain what surface rupture is.

name: Blind Faults
teaser: Blind faults are faults that don't reach the surface: they end below ground, hidden under folded sediment, yet they can produce devastating earthquakes — the 1994 Northridge quake in Los Angeles came from a blind thrust fault. The ground above folds as the fault slips, giving geologists clues to the buried structure. Blind faults are the hidden hazard: invisible until they rupture.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why some faults never reach the surface, then explain the Northridge quake lesson.

name: Fault Zones
teaser: A fault zone is the network of fractures and crushed rock around a fault: instead of a single clean crack, faults often branch and braid through a band of broken, ground-up rock called gouge and breccia. The zone can be meters to kilometers wide. Motion distributes across the zone, and its weak rock concentrates erosion, creating valleys. Fault zones are the full-width scars of plate motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why faults are zones not clean lines, then explain what gouge is.

name: Active Faults
teaser: Active faults are faults that have moved recently and are likely to move again: typically defined as having slipped within the last 10,000 years. They're mapped carefully because they mark where earthquakes will occur. Building codes, land-use planning, and insurance all hinge on active fault maps. The fault that moved yesterday is the one to worry about tomorrow.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how geologists judge a fault's activity, then explain what a recurrence interval is.

name: Folds and Faults
teaser: Folds and faults are the two ways rock responds to stress: rock bends into folds when it's warm and ductile, and breaks into faults when it's cold and brittle. The same mountain-building forces produce both — limestone folds into wavy layers, while granite cracks and faults. Depth, temperature, and rock type decide which happens. Reading folds and faults together reconstructs a region's deformation history.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn when rocks fold instead of break, then explain what controls the choice.

name: Strike and Dip
teaser: Strike and dip are the geologist's way of describing rock orientation: strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on a tilted layer, and dip is the angle and direction the layer slopes down. Measured with a compass and clinometer, they let geologists map tilted strata and folds. A sequence of strike-and-dip readings reveals the structure beneath. It's the language of structural geology.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how geologists measure rock tilts, then explain what a dip angle is.

name: Fault Scarps
teaser: Fault scarps are the step-like cliffs where a fault has moved the ground surface: one block rises or drops relative to the other, leaving a fresh slope — sometimes only a few meters high, sometimes hundreds. Repeated earthquakes build higher scarps. Scarps mark active faults and their recent motion. A fresh, sharp scarp is a sign of a recent quake.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how repeated slip builds scarps, then explain what a degraded scarp tells us.

name: Fault Creep
teaser: Fault creep is slow, continuous slip on a fault without earthquakes: some segments of the San Andreas, like those near Parkfield and Hollister, creep centimeters per year, steadily offsetting curbs and walls. Creeping segments release stress gradually, so they produce fewer large quakes, while locked segments build stress for big ones. The creep is measurable — fences and roads bend and break progressively.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how some faults move steadily, then explain why creep reduces quake size.

name: Mapping Faults
teaser: Fault mapping locates and characterizes faults: geologists trace fault traces, measure offsets, and date the displaced deposits to determine slip rates. Trenches dug across faults expose past ruptures, and geophysics images the underground structure. The maps show where future earthquakes are likely and how big they might be. Fault mapping is the foundation of seismic hazard assessment.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how geologists trace faults underground, then explain what paleoseismology is.

name: Paleoseismology
teaser: Paleoseismology digs into the past to find ancient earthquakes: geologists trench across faults and date the displaced layers — sand blows, faulted sediments, tilted deposits — to reconstruct past ruptures and their timing. The record shows earthquake cycles spanning thousands of years. Paleoseismology extends the seismic catalog far beyond written history. It tells us how often the big ones come.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how trenching reveals past quakes, then explain what offset layers show.

name: Faults and Cities
teaser: Faults and cities intersect where population meets hazard: San Francisco, Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul all straddle active fault systems. Urban faults raise risk — buildings over the rupture line can be torn apart, and infrastructure crosses the hazard. Cities respond with building codes, fault setback rules, and preparedness. Living on a fault means respecting its history and preparing for its future.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how cities plan around faults, then explain what setback rules are.

name: Faults and Water
teaser: Faults control groundwater: the crushed rock of fault zones can be either conduits or barriers — sometimes channeling water along the fracture, sometimes damming it behind impermeable gouge. Springs often emerge along faults, and wells target them for water. Faults also shape basins and aquifers. The same fractures that produce earthquakes can be the plumbing of the water supply.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how faults guide rivers and release springs, then explain what a fault spring is.

name: Engineering on Faults
teaser: Engineering on faults means designing for the inevitable: buildings near active faults use stronger frames, flexible foundations, and base isolation; pipelines get flexible joints; and critical facilities avoid fault traces entirely. Building codes specify how close to a fault construction may occur. The engineering is honest about the risk — you can't stop a fault, but you can build to survive it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how engineers design for quake risk, then explain what base isolation is.

name: Earthquakes
teaser: Earthquakes are sudden slips on faults: stress accumulates as plates move, the rock bends until it breaks, and the stored energy releases as seismic waves — shaking the ground. Most quakes happen at plate boundaries, but some strike within plates. Their size ranges from imperceptible rumbles to ground-splitting giants. Earthquakes are the Earth's way of adjusting, and they've shaped both geology and civilization.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what causes earthquakes, then explain why the ground suddenly moves.

name: Faults
teaser: Faults are fractures where rock has moved: stress from plate tectonics breaks rock and slides the blocks along the fault plane. The motion can be sudden — earthquakes — or slow creep. Faults come in normal, reverse, and strike-slip types, each reflecting different stress. Faults shape mountains, valleys, and coastlines. Nearly every earthquake is a fault moving.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how faults store and release stress, then explain what a fault plane is.

name: Elastic Rebound
teaser: Elastic rebound explains earthquakes: rocks bend like a spring as stress builds across a fault, storing elastic energy, until the rock breaks and snaps back — the rebound releases the energy as seismic waves. The theory was proposed after the 1906 San Francisco quake, which offset fences and roads. Quakes are the rock's spring finally letting go. The cycle of strain, slip, and rebound repeats endlessly.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how built-up strain releases as an earthquake, then explain the rubber-band model.

name: Hypocenters
teaser: The hypocenter, or focus, is the point inside Earth where an earthquake begins: the rupture starts here and spreads along the fault. Hypocenters range from shallow — a few kilometers, the most damaging — to deep — 700 kilometers in subducting slabs. The depth reveals the tectonic setting. Shallow quakes shake the surface hardest. The hypocenter is the earthquake's birthplace.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between hypocenter and epicenter, then explain where rupture begins.

name: Epicenters
teaser: The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above an earthquake's hypocenter: it's usually where shaking feels strongest, though the damage can extend far beyond. Seismologists locate epicenters by comparing P and S wave arrival times at multiple stations. Modern systems locate them in seconds. The epicenter is the address of the earthquake on the map.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the epicenter is located, then explain why damage peaks near it.

name: Seismographs
teaser: A seismograph is the instrument that records earthquakes: a mass suspended on a spring stays still while the ground shakes around it, and the relative motion is recorded — historically on paper drums, now digitally. The recording is a seismogram. Seismographs are so sensitive they detect quakes on the other side of the planet. They're the stethoscope of the Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how seismographs detect ground motion, then explain what a seismogram is.

name: Seismograms
teaser: A seismogram is the record of ground motion during an earthquake: it shows the arrival of P waves first — small, fast — then S waves, then the large surface waves that do most of the shaking. The time between P and S arrivals reveals the distance to the quake. The size of the wiggle indicates magnitude. A seismogram is the earthquake's signature written in ink.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how to read a seismogram, then explain how P and S arrivals differ.

name: Magnitude
teaser: Magnitude measures the energy released by an earthquake on a logarithmic scale: each whole number increase means about 32 times more energy — a 6.0 releases roughly 32 times the energy of a 5.0. Magnitude is determined from seismograms, independent of where you observe. The scale lets scientists compare quakes worldwide. Big numbers mean exponentially bigger events.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how magnitude scales measure energy, then explain why each step multiplies energy.

name: The Richter Scale
teaser: The Richter scale was the first magnitude scale, invented by Charles Richter in 1935 for California earthquakes: it measures the amplitude of seismic waves on a logarithmic scale, where each step represents a tenfold amplitude increase. It was designed for local, moderate quakes and has been replaced by the moment magnitude scale for large ones. But 'Richter' stuck in the public vocabulary for all magnitudes.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Richter measured quakes, then explain why modern scales replaced it.

name: Moment Magnitude
teaser: Moment magnitude is the modern scale for earthquake size: it measures the total energy released — the area of the fault that slipped, the amount of slip, and the rock's rigidity. Unlike the Richter scale, it works for the largest quakes and doesn't saturate. The 2011 Tohoku quake was 9.1; the 1906 San Francisco was about 7.9. Moment magnitude is the true measure of an earthquake's power.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how moment magnitude works, then explain why it suits huge quakes.

name: Intensity
teaser: Intensity measures the effects of an earthquake at a location, unlike magnitude's measure of energy: it's graded on the Modified Mercalli scale from I (barely felt) to XII (total destruction), based on shaking, damage, and human experience. Intensity varies with distance and local ground conditions. Maps of intensity show how shaking spread. Intensity is what people feel; magnitude is what the quake was.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the difference between magnitude and intensity, then explain what a Mercalli scale is.

name: Aftershocks
teaser: Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes following a main quake as the fault adjusts: the stress redistribution from the main rupture triggers slips on nearby patches. They can continue for days, months, or years, decreasing in frequency and size over time. Aftershocks complicate rescue and rebuilding, and can damage structures weakened by the main quake. They're the fault settling after the big slip.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why aftershocks follow main quakes, then explain why they can be dangerous.

name: Foreshocks
teaser: Foreshocks are smaller quakes that precede a larger one, hours to days before: they're the fault's first slips as stress approaches failure. Not all quakes have them, and they can't be reliably distinguished from ordinary small quakes until the main event happens. In hindsight, some big quakes — like the 2011 Tohoku event — show clear foreshock sequences. Foreshocks are a hint, but not a prediction.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why some quakes have foreshocks, then explain why they are hard to identify.

name: Earthquake Swarms
teaser: Earthquake swarms are sequences of many small quakes without a single large mainshock: they occur in volcanic areas, hydrothermal zones, and along some fault systems, where fluid movement or slow stress release triggers constant small slips. Yellowstone and Iceland have regular swarms. Swarms can last days to months. They're earthquakes in crowds rather than one big one.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how swarms differ from mainshock sequences, then explain what they may signal.

name: Where Earthquakes Happen
teaser: Earthquakes concentrate at plate boundaries: the Ring of Fire around the Pacific, the mid-ocean ridges, and the collision belts from the Mediterranean to the Himalayas host most of the world's quakes. Within plates, old fault zones still produce occasional events. The global map of quakes traces the plate edges. Knowing the zones tells societies where to prepare.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why most quakes hug plate boundaries, then explain the exceptions inside plates.

name: Intraplate Earthquakes
teaser: Intraplate earthquakes occur far from plate boundaries, inside stable continents: the 1811-12 New Madrid quakes in Missouri and the 1886 Charleston quake shook the US interior. They strike on ancient faults that reactivate under current stress, and they're rare but can be large. Because they're uncommon, they're poorly anticipated. Intraplate quakes remind us that even stable crust carries hidden faults.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why quakes occur inside plates, then explain what reactivated faults are.

name: Seismic Gaps
teaser: Seismic gaps are fault segments that haven't slipped in a long time while neighboring segments have: the quiet section may be locked, building stress for a future quake — the gap hypothesis. It helped forecast some events and failed others, so it's used as a guide, not a prediction. Gaps mark where the next big quake may be overdue. The fault's silence can be louder than its shaking.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how quiet fault segments hint at future quakes, then explain why gaps are studied.

name: Earthquake Early Warning
teaser: Earthquake early warning systems buy seconds of notice: sensors near the epicenter detect the fast P waves, and alerts race ahead of the slower, damaging S waves via radio and internet — giving people tens of seconds to drop, cover, and hold, and trains to stop. Japan, Mexico, and California have operating systems. The warning isn't prediction; it's outrunning the shaking.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how early warning systems work, then explain why seconds save lives.

name: Can Quakes Be Predicted?
teaser: Scientists cannot predict earthquakes — the exact time, place, and size remain beyond reach: the crust is too complex, and the processes are chaotic. What exists is forecasting — probabilities of quakes over years or decades based on fault history. Short-term prediction has failed every rigorous test. The honest science focuses on preparedness: build well, plan, and respond. The next big quake will come without a date on the calendar.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why quakes cannot be precisely predicted, then explain what probability forecasts mean.

name: Animals and Earthquakes
teaser: Animals behaving oddly before earthquakes is a popular claim with thin evidence: some studies show changes in bird roosts or dog behavior, but none reliably predict quakes. The anecdotes are retrospective — unusual animal behavior is common for many reasons. Sensors and physics outperform any animal. The search continues, but today the seismometer remains the only reliable quake detector.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what research says about animal behavior before quakes, then explain why evidence is mixed.

name: Earthquake Hazards
teaser: Seismic hazards are the dangers an earthquake can bring: ground shaking is the primary one, but liquefaction, landslides, tsunamis, and fires follow. The hazard depends on distance, local geology — soft soils shake more — and building quality. Hazard maps show where shaking will be strongest. Reducing the hazard means understanding the ground and building accordingly.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the hazards quakes create, then explain why ground shaking is the primary one.

name: Liquefaction
teaser: Liquefaction turns solid ground into a liquid during strong shaking: water-saturated loose sand loses its strength as the shaking jams grains apart, and buildings sink, tilt, or float while buried pipes rise. It strikes reclaimed land and river deltas — the 1989 Loma Prieta quake liquefied the Marina District. The fix is densifying the soil or anchoring deep foundations. Liquefaction is quake damage from the ground up.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how saturated soil liquefies in quakes, then explain why buildings tip over.

name: Quake Landslides
teaser: Earthquakes trigger landslides: shaking destabilizes steep slopes, sending rock and soil downhill — the 2008 Wenchuan quake in China triggered tens of thousands of landslides that killed many. Mountainous quake zones are doubly hazardous: first the shaking, then the collapse of hillsides. Landslide risk is mapped in quake-prone terrain. The shaking that breaks buildings can also move mountains.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how quakes trigger landslides, then explain why steep wet slopes are at risk.

name: Tsunamis
teaser: Tsunamis are ocean waves generated by sudden displacement of water — usually an undersea earthquake: the seafloor moves up or down, and the displaced water spreads as fast, low waves across the ocean, growing tall and destructive as they approach shallow coastlines. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 200,000 people. Tsunamis travel at jet speed in deep water and arrive as walls of water onshore. They're the earthquake's oceanic aftershock.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how quakes and landslides make tsunamis, then explain why they travel so fast.

name: How Tsunamis Work
teaser: Tsunami waves are different from wind waves: they involve the whole water column, travel hundreds of kilometers per hour in deep water, and have wavelengths of hundreds of kilometers. At sea they're barely a meter high; approaching shore they slow, pile up, and surge tens of meters inland. The first wave may not be the biggest, and water can recede before the surge. Tsunamis are the ocean responding to a shove from the Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why tsunamis grow tall near shore, then explain what a wave train is.

name: Tsunami Warning Systems
teaser: Tsunami warning systems detect the threat fast: seismometers flag quakes, deep-ocean pressure sensors detect the passing wave, and buoys relay the data to warning centers that issue alerts within minutes. The 2004 disaster lacked Indian Ocean coverage; now it exists. Evacuation to high ground is the lifesaver. The system's job is to convert earthquake data into a head start for the coast.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how buoys and models warn coasts, then explain why minutes matter.

name: Seismic Building Design
teaser: Seismic design makes buildings survive shaking: structures are engineered with strong frames, ductile joints that bend without breaking, shear walls, and moment frames that flex. The goal is to absorb and dissipate energy rather than resist it rigidly. Modern codes require this in quake zones, and well-designed buildings ride out quakes that level others. Seismic design is engineering with the earthquake in mind.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how buildings resist quakes, then explain what a shear wall is.

name: Base Isolation
teaser: Base isolation decouples a building from the ground: the structure sits on flexible bearings — rubber and lead pads — that absorb the shaking, so the ground moves beneath while the building sways gently. Isolated buildings can survive quakes that would destroy rigid ones. The technique protects hospitals, museums, and data centers — the 1994 Northridge quake left base-isolated buildings undamaged. It's the building equivalent of shock absorbers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how isolators decouple buildings from shaking, then explain what a bearing does.

name: Retrofitting
teaser: Retrofitting strengthens old buildings to survive quakes: weak first stories get steel frames, unreinforced masonry gets bracing, and foundations get bolting to the structure. Retrofits are cheaper than rebuilding and can be the difference between standing and collapse. Cities in quake zones — San Francisco, Los Angeles, Istanbul — are retrofitting the vulnerable stock. It's bringing yesterday's buildings up to today's standards.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how old structures get reinforced, then explain what a soft story is.

name: Earthquake Preparedness
teaser: Earthquake preparedness is the science of being ready: secure furniture, know safe spots, practice drop-cover-hold, and stock emergency supplies. Prepared communities respond faster and recover sooner. The quake itself takes seconds; the preparation takes years. Governments map hazards, schools drill, and families plan. You can't stop the shaking, but you can be ready for it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the drop, cover and hold advice, then explain why it saves lives.

name: Emergency Kits
teaser: Emergency kits are quake readiness in a bag: water, food, first aid, flashlight, radio, batteries, and medications for at least three days — plus copies of documents and cash. The kit should cover everyone in the household and be checked regularly. After a big quake, services can be disrupted for days. The kit is the difference between coping and struggling when the shaking stops.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what belongs in a quake kit, then explain why water tops the list.

name: Historic Earthquakes
teaser: Historic earthquakes read like a disaster catalog: Lisbon 1755 reshaped philosophy, San Francisco 1906 burned the city, Tangshan 1976 killed hundreds of thousands, and Tohoku 2011 triggered a nuclear accident. Each revealed new science — elastic rebound, liquefaction, tsunami dynamics — and drove building codes forward. The history of earthquakes is also the history of learning to survive them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the world's most famous quakes, then explain what each taught us.

name: The 1906 San Francisco Quake
teaser: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake was a landmark disaster: a magnitude 7.9 quake on the San Andreas Fault ruptured 430 kilometers, and the fires that followed destroyed most of the city. The quake killed thousands and gave geologists the elastic rebound theory of earthquakes. The city rebuilt on stricter standards. It also created the modern US seismic monitoring era.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the 1906 quake and fires destroyed San Francisco, then explain why it changed seismology.

name: The 2011 Tohoku Disaster
teaser: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake was a magnitude 9.1 event off Japan: the quake shifted the seafloor dramatically, generating a tsunami that overwhelmed seawalls and flooded the Fukushima nuclear plant, causing a meltdown. Nearly 20,000 people died, mostly from drowning. The disaster reshaped global thinking about extreme events — and showed that even well-prepared societies face limits. It also accelerated Japan's tsunami defense redesign.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the 2011 quake caused a massive tsunami, then explain the Fukushima link.

name: Great Earthquakes
teaser: Great earthquakes — magnitude 9 and above — are rare and enormous: the 1960 Chile quake was 9.5, the largest ever recorded, and 2004 Sumatra and 2011 Tohoku both reached 9.1. They occur only at subduction zones, where huge fault areas slip. Each released energy equivalent to thousands of nuclear bombs. Great quakes generate tsunamis that cross oceans. Their rarity is the only mercy.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what it takes to be a great quake, then explain why they happen at subduction zones.

name: Shaking Maps
teaser: Isoseismal maps trace lines of equal shaking intensity around an earthquake: drawn from reports of damage and felt shaking, they show how the quake's energy spread — typically elongated along the fault. The maps reveal which ground amplified the shaking and where the damage concentrated. Comparing intensity maps across quakes improves hazard mapping. They're the earthquake's felt footprint.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how shaking maps guide response, then explain what an isoseismal line is.

name: Earthquake Insurance
teaser: Earthquake insurance shares the risk of ground shaking: policies cover damage, but quakes are excluded from standard homeowners' insurance and require separate coverage with high deductibles. Insurers price risk from hazard maps and building quality. In high-risk zones like California and Japan, coverage is common but costly. After a big quake, insurance is what lets communities rebuild.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how quake insurance works, then explain why premiums vary by zone.

name: Building Codes
teaser: Building codes are the legal expression of seismic science: they specify how structures must resist lateral forces, from foundation anchorage to wall bracing. Codes are updated after each quake reveals weaknesses — the lessons become requirements. Strong codes are the cheapest earthquake insurance ever devised. Buildings that follow them routinely survive quakes that destroy those that don't.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how codes have made cities safer, then explain what a seismic code addresses.

name: Recovering From Quakes
teaser: Recovering from an earthquake is a multi-year process: immediate rescue and relief give way to restoration of power, water, and transport, then to rebuilding — ideally better than before. Recovery is a social and economic marathon shaped by insurance, governance, and memory. Communities that rebuild with stronger codes recover more completely. The earthquake is a moment; recovery is a generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the phases of disaster recovery, then explain why resilience takes decades.

name: The Next Big One
teaser: The 'next big one' is a forecast, not a prediction: geologists estimate that California faces a large quake on the southern San Andreas or the Hayward Fault within decades, with specific probabilities. The science identifies where and how big, not when. Preparation — retrofits, early warning, insurance — is the response to an uncertain clock. The next big one will come; the question is readiness.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why scientists expect future great quakes, then explain what scenario planning is.

name: Mountain Building
teaser: Mountain building, or orogeny, happens where tectonic plates collide or converge: continental collisions crumple and thicken crust into ranges like the Himalayas, subduction raises volcanic arcs like the Andes, and rifting leaves fault-block ranges. Mountains grow as plates push, and they're simultaneously eroded by rivers, glaciers, and weather. A mountain range is a competition between uplift and erosion.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the processes that build mountains, then explain what orogeny means.

name: Orogeny
teaser: Orogeny is the process of mountain building: a collision or subduction event that deforms, folds, faults, and thickens the crust over millions of years — the Appalachians, Alps, and Andes each formed through an orogeny. The result is folded rock, metamorphism, and uplift. Orogenies are recorded in the rock record and date the assembly of continents. Mountains are the scars of ancient plate collisions.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how plate collisions build mountain ranges, then explain what an orogen is.

name: Fold Mountains
teaser: Fold mountains form when compressional forces bend rock layers into waves: the Appalachians, Alps, and Himalayas are fold ranges, built from layers crumpled by plate collision. The folds — anticlines and synclines — can be kilometers across, and erosion carves the folded structure into ridges and valleys. Fold mountains reveal the deformation history of their rock. They're the classic mountain shape.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how crust folds into mountain ranges, then explain the Appalachian example.

name: Fault-Block Mountains
teaser: Fault-block mountains form where the crust stretches and blocks tilt along normal faults: the Sierra Nevada and the Basin and Range ranges rose as blocks tilted on faults, with valleys dropping between them. The steep face is the fault scarp; the gentle back slope is the tilted block. Extension, not collision, builds them. Fault-block mountains are the signature of stretched crust.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how extension tilts crustal blocks, then explain what a horst and graben are.

name: Volcanic Mountains
teaser: Volcanic mountains build themselves from erupted material: stratovolcanoes like Fuji pile lava and ash into steep cones, shield volcanoes like Mauna Kea spread broad slopes, and calderas collapse into great depressions. They form where magma reaches the surface — subduction zones, hotspots, and rifts. Volcanic mountains grow quickly in geologic terms. They're the youngest mountains, built from the inside out.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how repeated eruptions build peaks, then explain why they stand alone.

name: Folded Strata
teaser: Folded strata are rock layers bent into wavy forms by compression: originally horizontal beds — deposited flat — are squeezed into anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds) during mountain building. The folds record the direction and intensity of the force. Erosion exposes them as wavy ridges and valleys. Folded strata are the visible handwriting of crustal compression.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how layers fold without breaking, then explain what an anticline is.

name: Anticlines and Synclines
teaser: Anticlines are upfolds and synclines are downfolds in rock layers: anticlines arch upward — often trapping oil and gas in their crests — while synclines bow downward, collecting water and sediment. Together they form the ripple pattern of folded mountain belts. Erosion can invert them: a resistant syncline may stand as a ridge while a weak anticline erodes to a valley. Folds are the Earth's slow waves in stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the two fold directions, then explain how they trap oil and gas.

name: Isostasy
teaser: Isostasy is the buoyancy balance of the crust floating on the denser mantle: like an iceberg, mountains have deep roots and the crust rises or sinks to stay in equilibrium. Erode a mountain and it rebounds upward; pile on ice or sediment and the crust sinks. Scandinavia still rises from the weight of Ice Age glaciers. Isostasy explains why the crust is in constant, slow vertical motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how crust floats on the mantle, then explain why mountains have deep roots.

name: Mountain Roots
teaser: Mountain ranges have deep roots: the thick crust beneath a range extends kilometers into the mantle, like an iceberg's keel, keeping the mountain buoyant. The root compensates for the mountain's weight — the higher the range, the deeper the root. The Himalayas have crust over 70 kilometers thick. Erode the mountain and the root rebounds, lifting the range further. Mountains float on the mantle.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why mountains need deep roots, then explain what rootless mountains are.

name: The Himalayas
teaser: The Himalayas are the youngest and highest mountains on Earth, formed by the collision of India and Asia about 50 million years ago — and still rising a few millimeters a year. The collision crumpled the crust into Everest (8,849 m) and the entire range. The mountain-building continues as India pushes north. The Himalayas also drive the monsoon and feed the great rivers of Asia. The range is a collision in progress.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how India's collision built the Himalayas, then explain why they keep rising.

name: The Alps
teaser: The Alps formed when Africa's plate collided with Europe starting about 30 million years ago: the collision squeezed the Tethys Sea floor up into a fold-thrust belt of peaks — Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn. The range is still rising while glaciers carve it. The Alps' folded rocks record the ancient sea that once covered the region. They're Europe's classic mountain range, built by plate collision.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the African and European plates built the Alps, then explain their fold structure.

name: The Andes
teaser: The Andes are the longest continental mountain range, running 7,000 kilometers along South America: they formed where the Nazca plate subducts beneath South America, feeding the volcanoes and uplifting the range. The Andes host the highest peak outside Asia and drive the rain shadow that creates the Atacama Desert. Subduction builds them and triggers their frequent earthquakes. The Andes are a subduction zone, raised to the sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how subduction raised the Andes, then explain their volcanic line.

name: The Rockies
teaser: The Rocky Mountains rose in several pulses, mainly from 80 to 40 million years ago, when flat-slab subduction of the Farallon plate thickened the western US crust: the range was later carved by glaciers into its jagged peaks. The Rockies stretch from Canada to New Mexico, rich in minerals that fueled the West's mining booms. They're young, dramatic, and still rising. The Rockies are the American West's backbone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Rockies formed, then explain the difference from the coastal ranges.

name: The Appalachians
teaser: The Appalachians are old mountains — their rocks formed over a billion years ago, and they were uplifted during collisions that built Pangaea 300 million years ago: once as high as the Himalayas, they've eroded to gentle ridges and valleys. Their folded rocks match ranges in Europe and Africa, evidence of the supercontinent. The Appalachians show what billions of years of erosion do to a mountain range.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the Appalachians are old and rounded, then explain what erosion did to them.

name: Mountain Erosion
teaser: Mountains lose to erosion: rivers carve valleys, glaciers grind peaks, and weather breaks rock — lowering ranges by millimeters to centimeters per year. The material washes to the sea, building deltas and sediment. A range's height is a balance between uplift and erosion, and when uplift stops, erosion steadily wins. The Appalachians are the eroded stumps of a once-great range. Every mountain is a work in progress, being taken down.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how water and ice carve mountains, then explain why mountains lose height.

name: Mountains and Weather
teaser: Mountains make their own weather: as air rises over ranges, it cools and condenses, dropping rain and snow on the windward side, while the leeward side stays dry — the rain shadow effect. That's why the Pacific Northwest is wet and the Great Basin is desert. Altitude also drops temperature and thins the air. Mountains are weather machines, channeling moisture into distinct climate zones.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why mountains make rain shadows, then explain what orographic lift is.

name: Tree Lines
teaser: The tree line is the altitude above which trees can't grow: cold, wind, and short seasons limit tree survival, and the boundary shifts with latitude and climate. Above it lie alpine meadows and tundra. The tree line is a visible climate gradient on every mountain. It also moves — rising with warming, falling with glaciation. The tree line is where climate draws a line in the landscape.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why trees stop at certain heights, then explain what alpine tundra is.

name: Plateaus
teaser: Plateaus are elevated, flat-topped regions of uplifted rock: the Colorado Plateau, the Tibetan Plateau, and the Deccan Plateau rose as broad crustal blocks, then rivers and canyons carved into them. They form through uplift without folding — flat layers lifted high. Plateaus preserve the rock record beautifully, since erosion cuts into them rather than crumpling them. The Grand Canyon is a plateau's interior revealed.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how plateaus form, then explain what the Tibetan Plateau is.

name: Mesas and Buttes
teaser: Mesas and buttes are flat-topped hills carved from plateaus: a resistant cap rock protects the soft layers beneath, so erosion eats the sides while the top survives — a mesa is wider than tall, a butte is taller than wide. They're common in the American Southwest. As the cap erodes, a mesa shrinks into a butte, then a spire. They're the desert's monuments to resistant rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how erosion carves mesas and buttes, then explain the difference between them.

name: Life on Mountains
teaser: Life on mountains changes with altitude: forests give way to meadows, then rock and ice, each zone shaped by temperature, moisture, and oxygen. Alpine plants hug the ground, animals like mountain goats and pikas specialize in thin air and steep terrain. The zones shift with climate. Mountains host distinct ecosystems stacked vertically — a compressed journey from foothill to tundra in a single climb.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how life changes with altitude, then explain what alpine adaptation means.

name: Rivers
teaser: Rivers are the Earth's great movers: they erode rock, transport sediment, and deposit it downstream, carving valleys and building deltas. A river's work shapes the landscape more than any other single process. Rivers also carry water and nutrients, supporting civilizations along their banks. From mountain headwaters to the sea, a river is geology in motion — the land, dissolving and rebuilding itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rivers shape landscapes, then explain why they are the great sculptors.

name: River Systems
teaser: A river system is the whole network of channels draining a region: headwater streams merge into tributaries, which join the main river flowing to the sea. The system includes its drainage basin — all the land feeding it. Each part does different work: steep headwaters erode, lowland channels deposit. The system is a branching network, like veins on a leaf, delivering water and sediment from the land to the ocean.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tributaries feed rivers, then explain what a watershed is.

name: Watersheds
teaser: A watershed is the area of land that drains into a river, lake, or ocean: every drop of rain in a watershed eventually flows to its outlet, and ridgelines mark the boundaries between watersheds. The Continental Divide splits North America's drainage between the Atlantic and Pacific. Watersheds are the natural units of water management — what happens upstream affects everything downstream.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how a watershed works, then explain where your water drains.

name: Drainage Patterns
teaser: Drainage patterns reveal the geology beneath: dendritic patterns — branching like tree limbs — form on uniform rock; rectangular patterns follow fractures and faults; trellis patterns trace folded ridges; and radial patterns radiate from volcanoes and domes. The pattern of streams on a map is a geological X-ray of the ground. Rivers find the weak lines in the rock and follow them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why rivers form branching or trellis patterns, then explain what a dendritic pattern is.

name: Meanders
teaser: Meanders are the sinuous curves of mature rivers: water flows fastest on the outside of a bend, eroding the bank, and slower on the inside, depositing sediment — so the bend migrates sideways over time. Meanders grow, shift, and occasionally cut off to form oxbow lakes. They're a river's way of wasting energy on a gentle gradient. Meanders are rivers meandering, literally, across their floodplains.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why rivers curve and migrate, then explain how oxbow lakes form.

name: Oxbow Lakes
teaser: Oxbow lakes form when a river meander cuts itself off: the river erodes through the narrow neck of a bend, abandons the loop, and the old channel becomes a crescent-shaped lake. Over time, sediment fills it in and it becomes a marshy scar. Oxbow lakes dot floodplains worldwide — the Mississippi's valley is full of them. They're frozen snapshots of a river's former path.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how meanders cut off to form oxbows, then explain what happens next.

name: River Erosion
teaser: Rivers erode in three ways: hydraulic action — the force of water — scours banks, abrasion grinds rocks against the bed, and solution dissolves soluble rock like limestone. The erosion deepens and widens valleys, and the sediment the river carries does most of the cutting. A river is a geological saw — water power plus rock grit. Over millions of years, rivers cut canyons and flatten mountains.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the ways rivers erode, then explain what hydraulic action is.

name: Waterfalls
teaser: Waterfalls form where a river crosses a resistant ledge or a sudden drop: hard rock erodes slowly while softer rock below is worn away, undercutting the ledge until it collapses — and the waterfall retreats upstream. Niagara Falls has retreated kilometers this way. Waterfalls mark the boundaries between rock types and the river's disequilibrium. They're temporary features in a river's long journey to grade.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how waterfalls form on hard rock, then explain why they migrate upstream.

name: Deltas
teaser: Deltas form where rivers meet the sea: the flow slows, sediment drops, and land builds out into the water — the Nile, Mississippi, and Ganges deltas. The deposits spread into lobes and channels that shift over time, building fertile, low-lying land. Deltas are among the most productive and populated regions on Earth. They're the river's geological signature, written in sediment at the coast.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how deltas build new land, then explain what distributaries are.

name: Floodplains
teaser: Floodplains are the flat, low land beside rivers that floods periodically: rivers overflow, depositing fertile silt, and the plain builds up over millennia. Floodplains support rich agriculture — the Nile and the Mississippi valleys — but flooding is inherent to them. Levees confine floods but starve the plain of new sediment. A floodplain is the river's land, claimed during high water.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rivers build and flood their plains, then explain why floodplains are fertile.

name: Levees
teaser: Levees are the raised banks along rivers — natural ridges built by repeated floods depositing sediment, or engineered walls for flood control: natural levees form as floodwater slows at the channel edge and drops coarse sediment. Artificial levees protect farmland and cities but can worsen floods downstream by speeding water. Levees represent the ancient trade-off: control the river or live with it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rivers build natural levees, then explain why engineering levees is risky.

name: Alluvial Fans
teaser: Alluvial fans form where a stream exits mountains onto flat land: the flow spreads and slows, dropping its sediment in a fan shape — like a delta on land. They're common at mountain fronts in dry regions, built by flash floods and debris flows. Fans are steep near the apex and gentle at the edges, and their deposits record the mountain's erosion. Many desert cities are built on old fans.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fans form where canyons open, then explain why they spread in arcs.

name: Braided Rivers
teaser: Braided rivers are networks of interlacing channels separated by gravel bars: they form where a river carries more sediment than it can move and flows on steep gradients — glacial melt streams and mountain rivers are classic examples. The channels constantly split and rejoin as bars shift. Braided rivers are dynamic, unstable, and full of sediment. They're rivers with too much load and not enough flow.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why some rivers braid, then explain what sediment load does.

name: River Terraces
teaser: River terraces are step-like platforms along valley sides, marking former floodplain levels: when a river downcuts — due to uplift or base-level change — it abandons its old floodplain, leaving a terrace above the new channel. Repeated downcutting creates staircases of terraces. Terraces date past river levels and climate shifts, and they offer flat land for farming and cities. Each terrace is a former valley floor.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how terraces record river history, then explain what downcutting is.

name: Groundwater
teaser: Groundwater is water stored in the pore spaces and fractures of rock and sediment: rain infiltrates the ground and slowly moves through aquifers, emerging at springs, wells, and rivers. Groundwater supplies nearly half the world's drinking water and most irrigation. It's hidden but vast — more fresh water than all surface lakes and rivers combined. Groundwater is geology's most valuable resource, and it's being drawn down worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rain becomes groundwater, then explain what an aquifer is.

name: Aquifers
teaser: Aquifers are underground layers of rock or sediment that hold and transmit water: porous sandstone, gravel, and fractured limestone make good aquifers, while clay and shale act as barriers. Water fills the pores and flows slowly between grains. Aquifers range from shallow local sands to giant regional systems like the Ogallala. They're natural reservoirs — recharged by rain and drained by wells.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how aquifers store and release water, then explain the difference from aquitards.

name: Springs
teaser: Springs are where groundwater emerges at the surface: they occur where the water table meets the ground, where aquifers are cut by valleys, or where faults channel water upward. Springs range from seeps to gushing outlets, and their temperature depends on depth — hot springs are heated by deep rock. Springs have sustained human settlements for millennia and reveal the hidden plumbing of the subsurface.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why groundwater surfaces at springs, then explain what artesian springs are.

name: The Water Table
teaser: The water table is the underground boundary between saturated and unsaturated ground: above it, pores hold air and water; below, they're full of water. The water table rises with rain and falls with drought and pumping, and it mirrors the surface topography — high under hills, low in valleys. Wells must reach below it. The water table is the surface of the Earth's largest reservoir, rising and falling like a slow tide.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the water table rises and falls, then explain what overpumping does.

name: Aquifer Depletion
teaser: Aquifer depletion happens when pumping exceeds recharge: the water table drops, wells run dry, and the land can sink — subsidence — as the drained pores compact. The Ogallala Aquifer in the US and aquifers in India and the Middle East are being drained far faster than they refill. Some deep aquifers are effectively fossil water — unrenewable on human timescales. Depletion is the slow-motion emptying of Earth's savings account.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how pumping lowers water tables, then explain what land subsidence is.

name: River Restoration
teaser: River restoration reverses the damage of channelization: straightened, leveed rivers are returned to meandering courses with natural banks, floodplains, and wetlands. The goal is to restore the river's ecology and its natural sediment and flood dynamics. Restored rivers reduce flood peaks, rebuild habitat, and recharge groundwater. It's geology applied in reverse — letting the river be a river again.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how engineers restore natural rivers, then explain why straightening backfired.

name: Deserts
teaser: Deserts are regions that receive little precipitation — under 250 mm a year: they form where dry air dominates, from rain shadows, cold ocean currents, subtropical high-pressure belts, or high latitudes. Contrary to myth, most deserts aren't sandy — they're rocky, gravelly, or icy. Life in deserts adapts to water scarcity. Deserts are the Earth's driest geology, and they cover about a third of the land.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how deserts form and spread, then explain what defines a desert.

name: Types of Deserts
teaser: Deserts come in several types: subtropical deserts like the Sahara form under dry high-pressure belts; rain-shadow deserts like the Mojave sit behind mountains; coastal deserts like the Atacama face cold currents; and polar deserts are cold and dry — Antarctica is the largest. Each type forms by a different atmospheric mechanism. Deserts aren't all hot, and they aren't all sand. They're simply the places where water rarely falls.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rain shadows, latitude and cold create deserts, then explain what a subtropical desert is.

name: Rain Shadows
teaser: Rain shadows are dry zones on the leeward side of mountains: moist air rises over the range, cools, and drops its rain on the windward slopes; the air descending the other side is dry and warms, evaporating moisture. The Pacific Northwest's wet coast and dry interior, and the Atacama behind the Andes, are rain shadows. Mountains wring out the clouds and leave deserts behind them.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how mountains block rain, then explain why one side is green and the other dry.

name: Wind Erosion
teaser: Wind erodes in dry regions: it lifts loose sand and dust, abrades rock with airborne grains, and transports material great distances — dust from the Sahara reaches the Americas. Wind sculpts yardangs, polishes desert pavement, and builds dunes. Unlike water, wind can't carry heavy material far, but over millennia it shapes vast landscapes. Wind erosion is the desert's slow sculptor.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how wind removes and shapes sediment, then explain what deflation is.

name: Sand Dunes
teaser: Sand dunes are hills of windblown sand: they form where wind deposits sand around an obstacle, then grow as sand accumulates on the slip face. Dunes migrate downwind as grains saltate — bounce — up the gentle side and avalanche down the steep one. They come in crescents, ridges, and stars, shaped by wind direction and sand supply. Dunes are the desert's moving mountains.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how dunes form and migrate, then explain what a dune slip face is.

name: Types of Dunes
teaser: Dunes come in shapes determined by wind and sand supply: crescent barchans form in steady winds on hard ground, linear seifs stretch parallel to strong winds, star dunes grow where winds shift, and parabolic dunes anchor at vegetation. Each type records the wind regime. Dune fields can be vast — the Sahara and Rub' al Khali hold seas of sand. The shape of a dune is the wind's signature in sand.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why dunes form crescents, ridges and stars, then explain what a barchan dune is.

name: Yardangs
teaser: Yardangs are streamlined ridges carved by wind: elongated, keel-shaped hills of soft rock, aligned with the prevailing wind and sharpened like ship hulls pointing into the flow. They form where wind abrasion scours weak rock into parallel ridges — found in deserts from Egypt to the Atacama. Yardangs can be meters to kilometers long. They're the desert's wind-shaped sculptures.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how wind sculpts yardangs, then explain what ventifacts are.

name: Desert Pavement
teaser: Desert pavement is a surface of closely packed pebbles covering the ground: wind removes the fine sand and silt, leaving a mosaic of stones that armor the surface beneath. Over time the pavement protects the underlying sediment from further erosion. It forms slowly, and disturbing it can trigger dust storms — the Dust Bowl lesson. Pavement is the desert's natural armor.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how wind leaves a pavement of pebbles, then explain the puzzle of how it stays.

name: Mushroom Rocks
teaser: Mushroom rocks are wind-sculpted boulders with wide tops and narrow bases: windblown sand abrades the lower part — where the sand is concentrated — while the upper rock stays protected, carving a pedestal shape. They form in deserts with strong, sand-laden winds. Some are balanced on tiny stems, weathering into hoodoos over time. Mushroom rocks are the desert's sand-blasted towers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how wind-carried sand undercuts rocks, then explain their tops.

name: Oases
teaser: Oases are fertile spots in deserts fed by water: groundwater reaches the surface at springs, or wells tap shallow aquifers, supporting vegetation and settlement in otherwise barren land. Oases have been crossroads of desert trade for millennia — the Sahara's caravan routes linked them. They depend on finite groundwater and are vulnerable to overpumping. An oasis is where the desert's hidden water surfaces.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how water creates oases, then explain why they mark trade routes.

name: Playas
teaser: Playas are flat, dry lake beds in desert basins: when desert lakes evaporate, they leave smooth, salty flats — sometimes coated with salt crusts like Bonneville's race track. Playas form where water collects but can't drain, and they flood and dry seasonally. Their flatness and hard surface make them natural speedways and landing strips. Playas are the desert's vanished lakes, dried to a crust.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how lakes vanish into playas, then explain what salt flats are.

name: Badlands
teaser: Badlands are dramatically eroded landscapes of soft sedimentary rock: steep, dissected slopes cut by flash floods into intricate gullies and spires, with colorful banded layers — South Dakota's Badlands and the Painted Desert are examples. The rock erodes fast, exposing fossils and forming a maze of ridges. Badlands are geology at maximum speed, carved by water into miniature canyons.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how flash floods carve badlands, then explain why the name fits.

name: Desertification
teaser: Desertification is the degradation of dry land into desert-like conditions: overgrazing, deforestation, and poor farming strip the soil, and wind and water erosion complete the job — the Sahel's creeping sands are the classic case. It's not advancing sand dunes as much as losing productive land. Restoration — planting, terracing, water management — can reverse it. Desertification is human-driven geology going wrong.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how humans and climate dry out land, then explain what overgrazing does.

name: Loess
teaser: Loess is windblown silt that blankets large regions: glacial grinding and desert winds produce fine dust that settles into thick, fertile deposits — the Chinese Loess Plateau is hundreds of meters deep. Loess is rich in nutrients and drains well, making it some of the world's best agricultural soil, but it erodes easily when exposed. Loess is the desert's gift and hazard, a soil built from airborne dust.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how wind piles up loess, then explain why its soils are fertile.

name: Desert Water
teaser: Deserts and water are not opposites: flash floods carve desert canyons, groundwater feeds oases, and ancient lakes once filled desert basins. Rain that does fall runs off quickly over hard, bare ground, causing violent floods. Dry riverbeds — wadis — fill and rage after storms. Water, even rare, shapes deserts more than wind does. The desert is a place where water arrives suddenly and leaves fast.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how deserts get water, then explain what flash floods are.

name: Life in the Desert
teaser: Desert life adapts to water scarcity through chemistry and behavior: cacti store water and photosynthesize at night, kangaroo rats never drink — they get water from seeds — and reptiles and insects minimize water loss. Plants use deep roots, waxy coatings, and CAM photosynthesis. The adaptations are biological chemistry tuned to aridity. In the desert, water conservation is the whole game of survival.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how plants and animals cope with dryness, then explain what xerophytes are.

name: The Sahara
teaser: The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert, spanning North Africa — nearly the size of the US: it was once grassland with lakes and rivers, drying over the past several thousand years. Its dunes, rocky hamadas, and vast ergs record long climate cycles. The Sahara's dust fertilizes the Amazon, crossing the Atlantic on trade winds. It's a desert that was green, and may be green again.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Sahara formed and changes, then explain what the green Sahara was.

name: The Gobi
teaser: The Gobi is a cold desert in Asia, straddling Mongolia and China: it lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, and its winters are freezing — it's a desert of extremes. The Gobi holds dinosaur fossil beds — the first dinosaur eggs were found there — and it's one of the world's fastest-expanding deserts, threatening the land with desertification. The Gobi is a desert shaped by cold and dust storms.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the Gobi is cold and dry, then explain what fossils it hides.

name: Deserts and Climate
teaser: Deserts respond to climate change: warming expands subtropical deserts, the Sahara's edge advances and retreats with rainfall, and drier conditions increase dust storms and fire risk. Some deserts are greening in a warmer, wetter world while others expand. The feedback runs both ways — desert dust affects climate. Deserts are dynamic, climate-sensitive systems, not static wastelands.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how climate change affects deserts, then explain why dry lands may expand.

name: Exploring Deserts
teaser: Deserts have been explored by trade, science, and survival: caravans crossed the Sahara and Gobi for millennia, linking civilizations; explorers mapped them in the 1800s; and today satellites monitor them. Deserts preserve human history — mummies, rock art, and cities buried in sand. Their harshness tests both people and equipment. Exploring deserts is geology and history in the same harsh classroom.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how people have crossed deserts, then explain why water decided the routes.

name: Glaciers
teaser: Glaciers are slow-moving rivers of ice that form where snow accumulates faster than it melts: the weight compresses snow into dense ice, which flows downhill under its own pressure. Glaciers erode mountains, carve valleys, and deposit debris. They cover about 10% of Earth's land and store most of its fresh water. Glaciers are the largest geological agents of erosion on the planet.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what glaciers are and why they move, then explain the difference from frozen lakes.

name: How Glaciers Form
teaser: Glaciers form where winter snow exceeds summer melt: year after year, the snow piles up, compressing under its own weight — air is squeezed out, and snow recrystallizes into dense glacial ice. When the ice is thick enough, it begins to flow under gravity. The transformation takes decades to centuries. A glacier is snow that survived and turned to flowing rock-hard ice.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how snow becomes glacier ice, then explain what firn is.

name: Glacier Movement
teaser: Glaciers move by internal deformation and basal sliding: the ice grains deform and creep under pressure, and where the base is wet, the glacier slides over its bed. Movement is slow — centimeters to meters a day — but relentless. The ice flows faster in the middle than at the edges, and surges can accelerate dramatically. A glacier is a river of ice moving on geological timescales.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why glaciers flow, then explain the difference between plastic and basal flow.

name: Valley Glaciers
teaser: Valley glaciers are rivers of ice confined to mountain valleys: they flow downhill from snowfields, eroding the valleys they occupy into deep, U-shaped troughs. They sculpt cirques, arêtes, and horns at their heads and deposit moraines at their snouts. Valley glaciers are the sculptors of alpine landscapes — the Matterhorn and Yosemite's cliffs were carved by them. They're alpine ice in motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how valley glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, then explain why they follow valleys.

name: Ice Sheets
teaser: Ice sheets are the largest glaciers — continent-scale ice masses covering Greenland and Antarctica: they're kilometers thick, hold most of Earth's fresh water, and flow slowly outward from central domes. Their weight depresses the crust beneath them. Ice sheets store a record of past climates in their layers. If they melted entirely, sea level would rise over 60 meters. They're the planet's frozen giants.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how ice sheets cover entire regions, then explain the difference from glaciers.

name: Ice Caps
teaser: Ice caps are dome-shaped ice masses smaller than ice sheets but larger than glaciers: they cover highlands and islands — Iceland's Vatnajökull is an example — and they flow outward in all directions. Ice caps can blanket entire mountain ranges, hiding the peaks beneath. Their melt feeds rivers and raises sea level. Ice caps are miniature ice sheets, frozen reservoirs in the cold corners of the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ice caps differ from sheets, then explain what an icefield is.

name: Glacial Erosion
teaser: Glaciers erode by plucking and abrasion: ice freezes onto bedrock and pulls blocks loose — plucking — while the rocks frozen into the ice's base grind the bedrock like sandpaper — abrasion. The result is polished, striated rock and deepened valleys. A glacier is a slow, powerful rasp carrying its own tools. Glacial erosion reshapes entire mountain ranges over thousands of years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how glaciers erode bedrock, then explain what plucking is.

name: U-Shaped Valleys
teaser: U-shaped valleys are the signature of glacial erosion: rivers carve narrow V-shaped valleys, but glaciers widen and deepen them into broad, flat-bottomed U profiles as ice grinds the sides and floor. The hanging valleys, steep walls, and straight courses distinguish them from river valleys. Yosemite and the fjords of Norway are classic U-shaped valleys. The shape is a glacier's calling card.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why glaciers carve U shapes, then explain the difference from V-shaped river valleys.

name: Cirques
teaser: Cirques are bowl-shaped amphitheaters carved into mountainsides by glaciers: at a glacier's head, ice plucks and grinds the rock into a steep-walled basin. When the ice melts, the cirque may hold a tarn — a small lake. Cirques line the upper slopes of glaciated ranges, and adjacent cirques carve peaks into horns and ridges. They're the birthplaces of valley glaciers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how cirques form at glacier starts, then explain what a tarn is.

name: Arêtes
teaser: Arêtes are sharp ridges formed where two glaciers carved parallel valleys: as the glaciers eroded on both sides, the ridge between them was sharpened into a knife-edge crest. Arêtes are common in glaciated mountains, often connecting peaks and cirques. The Matterhorn's famous ridges are arêtes. They're the razor edges left where ice sculpted from two sides.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how two glaciers carve a ridge, then explain what a horn is.

name: Glacial Horns
teaser: Glacial horns are sharp, pyramidal peaks formed where three or more cirques carved a mountain from all sides: each cirque gnaws into the summit, and the remaining peak is a pointed horn — the Matterhorn is the classic example. Horns are the mountain's last stand against the glaciers. They're the most dramatic product of glacial erosion.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how several cirques carve a horn, then explain the Matterhorn example.

name: Hanging Valleys
teaser: Hanging valleys are tributary valleys perched above the main valley floor: glaciers deepened the main valley more than its tributaries, so when the ice melted, the side valleys were left high — ending in waterfalls that plunge into the main valley. Yosemite Falls and the waterfalls of fjords tumble from hanging valleys. They're the architectural signature of glacial valley carving.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why tributary valleys hang above main valleys, then explain the waterfalls they create.

name: Fjords
teaser: Fjords are U-shaped glacial valleys flooded by the sea: glaciers carved deep troughs below sea level, and when they retreated, the ocean filled them — Norway, Chile, and New Zealand have spectacular fjords. They're steep-walled, deep, and often connected to the open sea by shallow sills. Fjords are glaciated valleys drowning in the sea, and they're among the most dramatic landscapes on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how glaciers and rising seas make fjords, then explain what makes them deep.

name: Glacial Deposits
teaser: Glaciers deposit the debris they carry: unsorted mixtures called till are dumped directly by ice, forming moraines, while meltwater sorts and layers the sediment into outwash plains and eskers. The deposits include boulders, sand, and clay mixed together. Glacial deposits cover much of North America and Europe, left by Ice Age ice sheets. They're the fingerprints of vanished glaciers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how glaciers transport and drop debris, then explain what till is.

name: Moraines
teaser: Moraines are ridges of debris dumped by glaciers: terminal moraines mark the glacier's farthest advance, lateral moraines line its sides, and medial moraines form where tributaries merge. The piles of till — unsorted rock — are pushed and dumped at the ice margins. Moraines dam lakes, ridge landscapes, and record the glacier's history. They're the rubble walls left where ice stopped.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the types of moraines, then explain what a terminal moraine marks.

name: Glacial Erratics
